About the Author

Dr. Edward D Lavieri Jr. is a seasoned software developer and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE). He holds a Doctor of Computer Science from Colorado Technical University, a Master of Science in Information Systems from Bowie State University, and additional Master of Science degrees from the University of Arkansas at Fayetteville and Capella University. His experience spans the military, the software industry, and academia.

He has a firm understanding of modern software systems, based on his diverse practical experience—from working with intelligence and communication systems in the U.S. Navy to leading a software design and development studio. His vast professional experience includes working on various software projects, including grants from the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the U.S. Department of Education.

Dr. Edward’s industry experience and knowledge shine through his published works, which includes nearly two dozen technical books, numerous articles, and ongoing research. His deep engagement with modern technology is further demonstrated through his leadership roles in academia—serving as a University Dean for a College of Computer Science and a School of Information Technology, as well as the Chief Academic Officer for a programming bootcamp organization. These concurrent academic positions are part of a university system accredited by the Higher Learning Commission.

When not working on technical or academic projects, Dr. Edward Lavieri enjoys building new worlds with software and bricks.

Preface

Kickstart Java Programming Fundamentals is designed to empower readers with a deep understanding of the Java programming language, and modern software development techniques. Firstly, the book offers interactive exercises, allowing readers to apply principles in real-world scenarios, thereby solidifying their understanding of how software design directly impacts the efficiency, scalability, and maintainability of applications. Secondly, through an extensive collection of real-world examples, it provides industry's best practices, demonstrating the influence of well-designed software on a project’s success.

This book consists of 20 chapters, each a complete module, serving as your comprehensive guide to fully understanding applied Java programming fundamentals. It covers a wide array of topics, ranging from the fundamentals to advanced techniques. Whether you are a seasoned software developer looking to expand your skills, or a newcomer eager to dive into the Java programming language, this book has something for everyone. Each chapter concludes with points to remember, multiple choice questions (and answers), deep thought questions, key terms, and exercises.

Chapter 1 is your start to Java programming. It explores the language’s history, core features, and its ecosystem. You can gain exposure to Java’s rich set of libraries, its platform independence, and can discover the significance of Java across industries. Java truly is the cornerstone of modern software development, and the significance of your foray into Java has never been greater. This chapter guides you through setting up your Java development environment, and offers a first set of hands-on opportunities – you will write and run your first Java program! This chapter also introduces the syntax and structure that is used for all Java applications.

Chapter 2 is designed to help you learn how to declare and manipulate variables, work with different data types, and modify data using various operators. The chapter explores control structures—key elements that enable you to make decisions, and repeat actions within your programs. These topics are intended to extend your understanding of Java’s syntax, helping you write more dynamic and responsive code.

Chapter 3 is an introduction to Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), a fundamental paradigm in modern software development. It allows programmers to create modular, reusable, and maintainable code by organizing software into objects that represent real-world entities. This chapter examines the core concepts of OOP, including how to define, and use classes and objects, the building blocks of Java applications. The chapter explores how constructors are used to initialize objects, how inheritance allows us to extend existing functionality, and how polymorphism and method overriding provide flexibility in handling different types of objects. Encapsulation and abstraction, two critical OOP principles, have been explained in detail, demonstrating how they can help us manage code complexity, and improve code security and clarity.

Chapter 4 explores the various aspects of defining, calling, and managing methods in Java, including method overloading and recursion. You can learn about the significance of the static keyword when applied to methods. The chapter also introduces interfaces, which allow developers to set rules for what a class should do, without needing to focus on how it will be done. Understanding interfaces can enhance your ability to create flexible, and modular code by leveraging polymorphism, and clean design principles.

Chapter 5 explores two essential aspects of Java programming, such as file handling and exception handling. File handling is a fundamental skill that allows us to interact with external data sources by reading from and writing to files. The chapter explores how to work with text and binary files using Java’s file streams, and discusses the process of serialization and deserialization to efficiently store and retrieve complex data structures. Exception handling is a critical component in developing reliable and robust applications. This chapter demonstrates how to use Java to detect, and respond to runtime errors, ensuring that our programs can gracefully handle unexpected situations. From basic try-catch blocks to creating our own custom exceptions, this chapter presents the tools necessary to manage errors effectively, and improve the resilience of our Java applications.

Chapter 6 focuses on Java’s Input and Output (I/O) mechanisms which are critical for implementing data processing in Java applications. Coverage includes how to use Java I/O streams to efficiently read and write data from multiple sources (i.e., files, network connects, databases, and so on). This chapter explores the key types of streams—byte and character streams—alongside specialized buffered streams for optimized performance. Additionally, the chapter shows how data streams and object streams facilitate structured data handling. Finally, we will explore Java’s try-with-resources construct that streamlines resource management, and helps to ensure that system resources are properly closed after use.

Chapter 7 assists you ensure your applications work the way they are supposed to. Users expect software to work, but that is not enough; we also need to design and develop our applications, so that they are user-friendly and visually appealing. Those characteristics are key to the success of modern software. This chapter introduces Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) in Java with a focus on JavaFX, which is a powerful tool for building interactive Java applications.

Chapter 8 explores two concepts that are core to our ability to build high-performance and responsive Java applications: Concurrency and multi-threading. Regardless of the type of application we are developing, or our target system, understanding how to execute multiple computing tasks simultaneously from within our programs can result in great efficiencies, and a better user experience. The chapter also reviews foundational information and example code, so that our Java applications can take full advantage of modern systems with multi-core processors.

Chapter 9 introduces two critical concepts for modern efficient programming: Collections and data structures. They are applicable to large and small programs, and help us manage and organize our data. Mastering these concepts is essential for scalability and performance. This chapter introduces the Java Collections Framework, an important set of classes, and interfaces that help simplify the management of object groups. You can learn about various collection types, such as lists, sets, maps, and queues, and explore their specific use cases. Additionally, this chapter explains key algorithms like sorting and searching, so that you are able to process data efficiently.

Chapter 10 explores how Java can simplify the process of building robust and efficient networked applications through its comprehensive networking APIs. The chapter begins with an overview of networking in Java, and then focuses on the key concepts, such as sockets, which are the foundation for client-server communication. You can learn how to implement basic client-server models, work with different network protocols, such as Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), and handle advanced topics like multithreaded servers to manage multiple client connections. Additionally, the chapter demonstrates how to communicate over the web using HTTP connections and Java’s URL classes.

Chapter 11 focuses on databases which are at the heart of modern applications. They enable us to implement efficient and persistent data storage, data retrieval, and data management. This chapter explores how our Java applications can connect to relational databases, using Java Database Connectivity (JDBC). This provides a standard Application Programming Interface (API) for interacting with databases, making it easier to execute Structured Query Language (SQL) queries, retrieve data, and manage transactions. Whether you are building a simple application or a complex enterprise system, understanding JDBC is crucial for integrating data-driven functionalities into your projects.

Chapter 12 explores application performance, a critical aspect of modern Java applications. It is necessary to understand how to write code that works fast and efficiently. This chapter focuses on performance tuning and optimization techniques to help identify and address performance bottlenecks in Java applications. The chapter starts with an examination of profiling tools to measure and analyze the performance of our code. You can learn how to use these tools to pinpoint inefficiencies, and optimize your applications effectively. Memory management and the Java Virtual Machine’s garbage collection are also covered, as they are crucial for preventing memory leaks, and ensuring efficient resource usage. The chapter also introduces code optimization techniques to improve algorithm efficiency, and reduce overhead. Additionally, you can learn how to tune the JVM for better performance by adjusting various runtime parameters.

Chapter 13 covers Java’s robust set of security features, and testing and debugging tools, as well as focuses on three big and related concepts: How to build secure Java applications; how to efficiently test our applications, and debugging techniques. The chapter starts with a look at common security vulnerabilities and techniques for preventing them, using secure coding practices. Java’s built-in security APIs are covered to include encryption and access control. The chapter then transitions to testing and debugging with examples of efficient unit tests, Test-Driven Development (TDD) methodologies, and integrated debugging tools. Lastly, the chapter examines the role of automation, and continuous integration to help us maintain the quality of our application, throughout the development lifecycle.

Chapter 14 explores two of the most widely used Java frameworks: Spring and Hibernate. Spring is a popular framework that helps us implement dependency injection, aspect-oriented programming, and web development. Its infrastructure is ideal for building scalable applications. Hibernate, another popular framework, makes it easy for us to implement database interactions through an Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) framework. This chapter introduces Spring and Hibernate, demonstrates how to implement each one, and evaluates the benefits and drawbacks of using frameworks.

Chapter 15 explores Java web development with the intent to empower you to create scalable data-driven applications. Coverage starts with setting up a VS Code for a web development environment. Next, the chapter introduces fundamental Java web technologies, such as Servlets and Java Server Pages (JSP), to handle web requests and dynamic content generation. You will have the opportunity to integrate Spring Module-View-Controller (MVC) to create a structured and maintainable web application. The chapter also covers how to implement RESTful web services to enable communication between the frontend and backend. Application deployment on web servers ( for example, Apache Tomcat or Jetty) and the best practices are covered.

Chapter 16 explores the implementation of advanced programming constructs and language features to help increase the capability, interoperability, and efficiency of our applications. These features include lambda expressions, the Streams API, and the Optional container that can help modernize our Java applications. Also featured in this chapter, is cloud computing and functional programming which continues to grow in popularity as it can be used to help reduce the complexity of our code. These salient features will be explored with a goal of empowering you to write optimized Java applications that are scalable, efficient, and maintainable.

Chapter 17 focuses on developing mobile applications with Java. The target platform is Android, the most common mobile operating system. The chapter progressively builds a simple but functional to-do list application, JOLT (Java Organized List Tracker). The JOLT mobile application provides context to the concepts presented in this chapter, such as UI design, activity lifecycle, user interactions, and data persistence. The chapter also looks at cross-platform development.

Chapter 18 covers design patterns, and blueprints to guide our software design decisions. Using design patterns saves us considerable development time, and makes our code more readable and maintainable. This chapter also explores several foundational design patterns, based on the Gang of Four (GoF) classifications of creational, structural, and behavioral. We will cover several design patterns in each of the GoF classifications, and demonstrate key patterns with Java-based implementations.

Chapter 19 introduces foundational concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), and how to integrate those technologies into Java projects. You will have the opportunity to learn how to work with Java-compatible AI libraries, such as Deeplearning4j and Weka. The hands-on examples and practical exercises featured in this chapter can provide insight into how to train models, evaluate their performance, and use them to solve real-world problems. Natural Language Processing (NLP) will also be introduced.

Chapter 20 brings together everything the earlier chapters covered. This project-based chapter combines the concepts and techniques you gained exposure to throughout this book, into a complete Java application from the ground up. The final project is a desktop-based task management application called TaskWise AI. This application will allow users to add and manage tasks with a simple JavaFX interface, store those tasks in a local SQLite database, and apply a basic AI feature to automatically suggest task priorities, based on the task description.

Thus, this book is a hands-on guide filled with practical examples, real-world scenarios, and best practices. This journey through Kickstart Java Programming Fundamentals will empower you to design highly efficient, scalable, and maintainable systems, enhancing your skills in the dynamic field of software development. Happy Coding!

CHAPTER 1

Introduction to Java Programming

Introduction

This chapter is your start to Java programming. It explores the language’s history, core features, and its ecosystem. You will gain exposure to Java’s rich set of libraries, its platform independence, and can discover the significance of Java across industries. Java truly is the cornerstone of modern software development and the significance of your foray into Java has never been greater. This chapter guides you through setting up your Java development environment and offers a first set of hands-on opportunities – you will write and run your first Java program! This chapter also introduces the syntax and structure that is used for all Java applications. This chapter provides foundational knowledge to help you succeed in the chapters that follow.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to understand the history, key features, and ecosystem of Java, and set up a Java development environment using the JDK and an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). Furthermore, you will learn to write, compile, and execute a simple Java program, recognize and use basic Java syntax and structure, and explain the crucial role of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) in program execution.

Structure

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

  • Overview of Java and its Ecosystem
  • History and Evolution of Java
  • Setting Up the Development Environment (JDK, IDEs)
  • Writing and Running Your First Java Program
  • Basic Java Syntax and Structure
  • Introduction to the Java Virtual Machine (JVM)

Overview of Java and its Ecosystem

Let us get one thing straight from the very beginning; Java is an extremely powerful high-level programming language that is one of the mostly widely used programming languages on the planet. According to the Code Institute, 97% of enterprise desktops run Java, 89% computers in the U.S. run Java, 3 billion phones run Java, 125 million televisions run Java, and there are 9 million Java developers worldwide. Said another way, Java is a big deal! It was originally introduced in 1995 by Sun Microsystems and subsequently owned by the Oracle corporation.

Java’s premise is to write once and deploy anywhere, sometimes referred to as WORA. This is a powerful concept that allows us to write our Java code, not knowing what hardware platforms or operating systems it will be used with. The only requirement is that the deployment hardware and operating system support the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). We will discuss JVM later in this chapter. For now, think of it as the connective tissue between the Java programs we write and the system they are deployed on.

The ability to deploy our Java applications on any system that supports the JVM is why Java is characterized as portable. This portability continues to contribute to Java’s large-scale adoption in systems from embedded circuits to mobile applications, and desktop applications to cloud applications.

Key Features

Java is feature-rich, providing us with tremendous programming capabilities. Here is a list of six core features of the Java programming language. These are presented in alphabetical order so no level of importance should be gleaned from their order on this list.

  • Garbage Collection: Java includes a built-in automatic memory management system referred to as garbage collection. This system automatically manages memory allocation and deallocation. This saves us a lot of time and can make our applications more resource efficient and higher performant. We will take a close look at Java’s garbage collection in Chapter 12, Java Performance Testing and Optimization.
  • Object-Oriented: Java is a true object-oriented programming (OOP) language. That means everything in Java is represented as an object. This approach allows us to model real-world entities and build reusable modular code. You will have the opportunity to learn about the core OOP concepts of abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism in Chapter 3, Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Basics.

  • Platform Independence: One of the greatest advantages of using Java is that it is a platform-agnostic programming language, meaning it has platform independence. When we write our Java programs, we do not need to consider what platform it is. For example, we can write a Java application using a Windows computer and publish it for users regardless of whether their computers run Mac OS, Windows, or Linux. This is possible because, as depicted in Figure 1.1, our source code is converted to Bytecode by the Java Compiler, and then the JVM runs machine code on the deployment computer.

    Figure 1.1: Java Bytecode Process

  • Multithread: Multithreading allows for more than one thread to run concurrently. This is especially important with modern systems that have multiple CPUs. Each component of a running application is considered a thread. Java has strong support for multithreading. We will take a closer look at how to implement multithreading with Java in Chapter 8, Concurrency and Multi-Threading.
  • Secure: Modern programming languages should include features that help us create secure programs, and Java does not disappoint. Java includes features such as strong typing and exception handling to help prevent errors at runtime. In addition, the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) creates a secure application execution environment through the implementation of access controls. We will take a closer look at security in Chapter 13, Security, Testing, and Debugging.
  • Standard Library: Java’s Application Programming Interface (Java API) is extensive, providing developers with a rich set of ready-to-use functions for common tasks, such as networking, input/output operations, concurrency, Graphical User Interface (GUI) development, and much more. We can use these libraries to speed up our development. As you progress through this book, you will have the opportunity to explore much of Java’s rich standard library.

This feature list is a high-level overview of Java’s core features. You will have the opportunity to learn about these features as well as additional ones as you progress through the book.

Java’s Ecosystem

An ecosystem is a set of interconnected systems. The Java ecosystem is expansive and, as depicted in Figure 1.2, includes a wide range of components that collectively build a complex network of interconnected systems.

Figure 1.2: Java Ecosystem

Figure 1.2 includes nine components of the Java ecosystem. The following sections provide details on each of them and are organized into ‘core,’ ‘non-core,’ and ‘community’ categories.

Core

This section covers three core components of the Java ecosystem, including:

  • Java Development Kit (JDK): The Java Development Kit (JDK) is our core tool as Java developers. It contains the Java Compiler, the JRE (described in the next point), and tools that support our debugging and application management tasks. The JDK empowers us to write, debug, compile, and run Java programs. We cannot develop Java applications without it. The Setting Up Your Development Environment section of this chapter walks you through setting up the JDK so you can start programming in Java.
  • Java Runtime Environment (JRE):The JRE is part of the JDK and is what runs our Java applications. The JRE includes the JVM (described in the next point), core libraries, and more. As Java developers, we only need the JDK to create our Java programs; end users only need the JRE to run them.
  • Java Virtual Machine (JVM): As previously mentioned, the JVM is the reason Java is platform independent. It has the core responsibility of executing Java bytecode. JVM implementations are available for nearly every platform, meaning Java applications can be run almost everywhere. The JVM has additional responsibilities to include garbage collection, security, and just-in-time compilation. A full exploration of the JVM is provided in the Introduction to the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) section of this chapter.

Figure 1.3 shows the relationship between the JDK, JRE, and JVM.

Figure 1.3: Java Ecosystem Core Components

Non-Core

This section covers five important components of the Java ecosystem. They are listed as ‘non-core’ because there is more than one option for each of them. That does not mean they are optional components, rather, that for each one you have multiple options to choose from.

  • Integrated Development Environments (IDEs): IDEs are software applications that help us write, test, debug, and update our code. While we can use a simple text editor to create our Java programs, use of an IDE and its embedded tools represents tremendous efficiency for us. There are a lot of powerful IDEs available for Java development, both free and paid. Most IDEs support the develop of code in many different languages. The selected IDE used throughout this book is Visual Studio Code, which is free to use. The Setting Up Your Development Environment section of this chapter walks you through downloading, installing, and configuring Visual Studio Code.
  • Build Tools: Build tools can help simplify the process of managing dependencies, compiling our code, and packaging our applications. Build tools can be integrated directly into our IDE. Use of build tools is not required but is highly recommended for large-scale projects. The most common build tools are Ant, Gradle, and Maven.
  • Frameworks: Frameworks offer pre-built, ready-made functional components that we can use in our Java programs. There is a vast and growing number of frameworks that can streamline our development efforts. Each framework is typically aligned with a specific programming area, such as JavaFX for building Graphical User Interface (GUIs). We will take a deeper look at specific frameworks in Chapter 14, Exploring Popular Java Frameworks. In addition, we will work with JavaFX in Chapter 7, GUI Programming.
  • Libraries and APIs: Java has an impressive standard Application Programming Interface (API) and there is a voluminous number of third-party libraries we can use. Most of these libraries focus on a specialized task such as the Jackson library that can be used for parsing JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) data. As you progress through this book, libraries will be introduced so, by the end of this book, you will have exposure to a significant number of these libraries.
  • Application Servers: There are several types of servers such as web server, database server, and application server. The application server hosts applications and is common in enterprise and large-scale systems. The work of an application server includes transaction management, security, and scalability. The most common Java application servers are Apache Tomcat, JBoss, Jetty, and WebSphere. We will cover web servers in Chapter 15, Java for Web Development.

Community

This final component of the Java ecosystem consists of Java’s massive developer community, extensive documentation, developer forums, and open-source projects. Some of the more popular sites are listed here along with their URLs:

  • Geeks for Geeks: https://geeksforgeeks.org/java/
  • GitHub: https://github.com/topics/java
  • Oracle Java Documentation: https://docs.oracle.com
  • Stack Overflow: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/java

Java Editions

As a conclusion to our overview of Java and its ecosystem, it is important to note that there are three main editions of Java. As you can see in Table 1.1, each edition caters to different application types.

Edition

Abbreviation

Description

Standard Edition

Java SE

This is the core version of Java and the one we will use throughout this book. It provides the fundamental libraries and APIs we need for general-purpose application development.

Enterprise Edition

Jakarta EE

Jakarta EE was previously named Java EE until around 2017. This edition is used for large-scale, distributed systems. Enterprise applications are built with this edition. It includes libraries used for creating web services, servlets, enterprise-level messaging, and more.

Micro Edition

Java ME

This version is used for embedded systems, phones, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and other small systems.

Table 1.1: Java Editions

History and Evolution of Java

The first stable version of Java was released on May 23, 1995, making May 23, 2025, the 30th anniversary of this powerful programming language. It had an earlier start in 1991 when James Gosling, and a team of Sun Microsystems engineers, labored to revolutionize embedded systems.

As illustrated in Figure 1.4, there were four major periods in Java’s history that included its origin, formative years, rise of Java Enterprise, an expansion period, and then the current period that started when Oracle purchased Sun Microsystems and has shepherded the Java language ever since.

Figure 1.4: Timeline of Java’s Existence

Let us briefly look at each of these periods.

Java is Born (1991-1995)

Java was originally named Oak and was changed to Java as a reference to coffee. The engineering team aimed to create a language that was simpler than the then prominent C++ language, independent of any specific platform, that was secure, high performing, and supported multiple CPUs. Interestingly, Java was released as part of the Netscape Navigation web browser to enable Java applets to run on web pages. This catapulted interest in interactive web content and made Java an immediate success.

The Formative Years (1996-2000)

In 1996, the first Java Development Kit (JDK) was released, empowering developers to write and compile Java code. The software development community likely gravitated to Java because it could be used to develop applications in modular form and deploy them everywhere from a single code base.

During this period, there were key releases to include JDK 1.1 in 1997 and Java 2 (JDK 1.2) in 1998. The release of Java 2 included the split of Java into three editions as noted in Table 1.2.

Edition

Current Name

Purpose

J2SE

Java SE

General-purpose applications

J2EE

Jakarta EE

Large-scale, distributed applications

J2ME

Java ME

Embedded systems and mobile devices

Table 1.2: Java Editions

Notably, the Swing API was released during the formative years. Swing was used for building GUIs. In addition, the Collections Framework was released during this period and supported data structures.

Rise of the Enterprise (2000-2006)

Java became the predominant language for enterprise applications, with some focus on server-side development. Java support of multithreading and its object-oriented nature made it ideal for creating scalable distributed applications. There were two major releases during this period: Java 1.4 in 2002 and Java 5 in 2004. This later edition included key feature upgrades including generics, the enhanced for-loop, enumerations, and more.

Java’s Expansion (2006-2010)

The Java expansion period was 2006 through 2010 and started by Sun Microsystems releasing Java under the Gnu’s Not Unix (GNU) General Public License (GPL), commonly referred to as GNU GPL. This made Java open-source and opened the door to community developers to help further expand Java’s capabilities.

Java 6 was released during this period and included performance improvements along with other updates.

The Oracle Years (2010-Present)

The world of Java was forever changed in 2010 when Oracle purchased Sun Microservices, which included Java. Oracle has done a great job with continually improving the language. In fact, they shifted the 2-year release cycle to every 6-months. This aggressive release schedule has helped ensure new features were available sooner and incremental releases were not as large.

Java continues to evolve and remains relevant as a primary development tool for platforms of all types.

Setting Up Your Development Environment

We will take a two-step approach to setting up our development environment. Step one is to install the Java Development Kit (JDK) and step two is to install an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). All the software and tools featured in this section are free.

Step one is to install the JDK. For this step, we will first download the JDK, install it, verify our installation and then set our environmental variables. Here are the details of these actions:

  1. Use your browser to visit Oracle’s official JDK download page. Select the JDK version that matches your development computer’s operating system and CPU. For example, Figure 1.5 shows the settings for JDK 22 and a system running macOS.

    Figure 1.5: JDK Download Page with JDK 22 and macOS selected

    Note: At the time this book was written, Oracle’s official JDK download page was located at the provided URL. URLs can change and if this link is no longer valid when you read this book, please just search for “official Oracle JDK download page” via an internet search engine.

    https://oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads

  2. Once the download completes, run the installation wizard. You can generally accept all defaults during the installation process. If you are using a Windows system, you will see a check box labeled "Set JAVA_HOME variable" during the installation process. Be sure to check that box. This is handled automatically by macOS and Linux systems.

  3. Once the installation completes, we simply need to verify our installation. To accomplish this, we open a terminal window (macOS/Linux) or command prompt (Windows), type java -version, and hit the return button on your keyboard. The result should be like the following:

    java version "22.0.1" 2024-04-16

    Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 22.0.1+8-16)

    Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 22.0.1+8-16, mixed mode, sharing)

Our second step is to install our IDE. As previously mentioned, this book features Visual Studio Code (VS Code) as the IDE. This selection was made because it is free, lightweight, extensible, has powerful editing features, along with an integrated terminal. We will follow a four-step process: download, install, launch, and add extensions.

  1. Visit the https://code.visualstudio.com/download page and download the user installer specific to your development computer’s operating system. Figure 1.6 shows the download page with options for development systems running Windows, Linux, and macOS.

    Figure 1.6: VS Code Download Page

  2. Now that you have VS Code downloaded, run the installer, and follow the installation prompts. You can accept any default settings you might be presented with.
  3. Launch VS Code.

  4. Now we need to install Java extensions for VS Code. In the left column of the interface, you will see an icon with four blocks, one of them separate from the others. As illustrated in Figure 1.7, this is the bottom icon. Click that icon.

    Figure 1.7: VS Code Left Navigation

  5. In the extensions interface, search for 'Java extensions' and select the one from Microsoft named "Extension Pack for Java." Click the install button and complete the installation process.

That is all we need before we start writing Java programs. We will get started with our first Java program in the next section.

Note: If you need additional assistance downloading and installing Visual Studio Code and Java, you can visit the Visual Studio Code’s official sites listed here:

https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/windows

https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/java/java-tutorial

Writing and Running Your First Java Program

Now that your development environment is setup with the Java Development Kit (JDK) and Visual Studio Code (VS Code), you are ready to write and run your first Java program. This section provides a step-by-step guide to help you create a basic Java program, compile it, and run it within your IDE. The program will simply output a message to the console. This brief hands-on exercise is intended to introduce you to the process of Java development. First, let us review a few key terms:

  • Console: This is a window in the IDE where error messages and output are displayed.
  • Output: We can output text in the console window. This is also referred to as ‘printing to the console’ due to the use of the Java print method.

Follow these steps to complete the activity:

  1. Open VS Code.
  2. Create a new project folder. This can be done from within VS Code by opening the Explorer’s icon in the left sidebar, and then clicking Open Folder. This will engage your computer’s file system, allowing you to select an existing folder or create a new one.
  3. Now, in the File Explorer, select the project folder and click the New File button. Enter the name Main.java and press the return button on your keyboard.

  4. You will now have an active edit window with your Main.java file open. Enter the following code:

    public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

    System.out.println("Hello, Java Developer!");

    }

    }

    This simple program instructs Java to print "Hello, Java Developer!" to the console. For now, you do not need to be concerned about details of the code as we will exploit that in the next section.

  5. Next, we need to save our file. You can use the VS Code menu system or simply press Ctrl+S (Windows / Linux) or Cmd+S (macOS).

  6. Now, let us run our program. In the upper right-corner of the VS Code interface, click the Run icon (a right-pointing triangle outline) or press Ctrl+F5 (Windows) or Cmd+Cmd+F5 (macOS). The following should be visible in your console/terminal window:

    Hello, Java Developer!

This output confirms that your Java code worked and that your development environment is properly configured. To demonstrate what happened behind the scenes when you clicked the Run button, let us look at how this can be done manually.

  1. Inside VS Code, open a terminal window. This can be done by clicking the appropriate tab in the interface.
  2. You have already written the code in text form. Let us compile it into bytecode. This is done with the following command: javac Main.java. This generates a Main.class file, which contains our program's bytecode.
  3. To run the program, from within the terminal window, we use the following command: java Main

  4. The following output should be displayed in your terminal window:

    Hello, Java Developer!

In this section, we wrote and ran a simple Java program. These are important first steps on our Java development journey. In the next section, we will explore Java's basic syntax and structure, and examine how Java programs are organized, how to declare variables, use control statements, and more.

Basic Java Syntax and Structure

In the previous section, you created a simple Java program by typing in code that was provided. It is important that you understand Java's syntax and structure. This section covers the basics of syntax and structure to include how we define classes, methods, variables, control structures, and in-code comments in Java. We cover the basics in this section as building blocks for the chapters that follow.

Basic Structure

All Java programs are structured around classes and methods. Every Java program must have at least one class and, within that class, contain a main() method. This method serves as the starting point for the program's execution. Here is what that structure looks like:

public class Main {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// We enter code to be executed starting here.

}

}

Let us take a closer look at the class and method components of this structure. Here is our same preceding code, but with line numbers for easy reference.

1. public class Main {

2.    public static void main(String[] args) {

3.        // We enter code to be executed starting here.

4.    }

5. }

Line 1 is our class definition. All Java programs are made up of one or more classes. Our program’s class is named Main. The public keyword on this line indicates that the class is accessible by other classes. Of note, the class name must match the filename (Main.java).

Line 2 declares our main method. This is the starting point for all Java programs. The main() method is where the program execution starts. The String[] args allows us to pass command-line arguments to the program.

Line 3 contains a comment and is where we would start entering our own code.

Line 4 contains a closing curly bracket that is paired with the opening curly bracket at the end of line 2.

Line 5 contains a closing curly bracket that is paired with the opening curly bracket at the end of line 1.

We will spend a lot of time writing similar statements throughout the book, giving you ample opportunity to become extremely used to them. We will cover classes in Chapter 3, Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Basics and methods in Chapter 4, Methods and Functions.

Basic Syntax

We will now look at some basic syntax components to include comments, variables and data types, variable declaration and initialization, and constants.

Comments

Java allows us to write notes alongside our code. These are non-executable lines of code used to describe the code. This helps us when we need to troubleshoot and update the code. It also helps other developers understand your code in case they are performing quality assurance testing, integrating with it, or taking responsibility for it.

There are three types of comments in Java:

  1. Single-line comments begin with // and extend to the end of the line. They can be on their own line or at the end of a line of code. Here are two examples:

    // This is a single-line comment

    System.out.println(Total); // This is a single-line comment following a line of code

  2. Multi-line comments begin with /*, span multiple lines, and end with */. Here is an example:

    /*

    This is a multi-line comment

    that spans two or more lines.

    */

  3. Javadoc comments allow us to create descriptions for classes, methods, interfaces, and more. Javadoc comments are generated into html form. This will be covered in Chapter 16, Advanced Java Features.

Variables and Data Types

Variables are used to store data that our application can manipulate. Java requires that every variable be assigned a specific type. Data types define what kind of data the variable can hold. Java has primitive and non-primitive data ty public class Control {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// example if-else statement

int age = 16;

if (age >= 18) {

System.out.println(“You are old enough for this ride.”);

} else {

System.out.println(“You are not old enough for this ride.”);

}

// example switch statement

int jersey = 8;

switch (jersey) {

case 8:

System.out.println(“Kobe’s original jersey.”);

break;

case 24:

System.out.println(“Kobie’s newest jersey.”);

break;

case 32:

System.out.println(“Magic’s jersey.”);

break;

default:

System.out.println(“Jersey not found.”);

break;

}

pes.

In Java, non-primitive data types are those that are defined by the developer. These are complex data types such as Strings and arrays that are managed as objects. An example String is shown here as a sequence of characters and treated as an object.

String message = "Hello, Java Developer!";

Variables and data types are covered in detail in Chapter 2, Variables, Data Types, Operators, and Control Structures.

Variables Declaration and Initialization

To use variables in Java, we must declare and initialize them. Here is a variable declaration, where we are declaring that variable jersey is an integer (int).

int jersey; // this is a declaration

Once a variable is declared, we need to initialize it by giving it a value. Here is an example:

jersey = 24; // this is initialization

We can also combine these two actions into one:

int jersey = 24; // declaration and initialization

Constants

A constant is a value that cannot be changed after it is set. We use the final keyword as shown:

final double PI = 3.14159;

Operators

In Java, we use operators to perform actions on our variables to include arithmetic operations, comparison operations, and local operators.

Arithmetic Operators

We use arithmetic operators to perform mathematical operations. These are straightforward and are listed in Table 1.4 with examples.

Operator

Mathematical Operation

Example

+

Addition

sum = num1 + num2;

-

Subtraction

profit = sales – expenses;

*

Multiplication

product = num1 * num2;

/

Division

share = items / people;

%

Modulus (remainder)

remainder = num1 % num2;

Table 1.4: Java Arithmetic Operators

The arithmetic operators are likely familiar to you except for modulus, which simply provides the remainder of division operations. Let us look at an example. The following code uses four int variables and uses both the division and modulus operators:

int items = 17;

int people = 3;

int share = items / people;

int remainder = items % people;

The results of these operations are that share equal 5, based on 17 divided by 3, and remainder equals 2 because after 17 is divided by 3, there is a remainder of 2.

Comparison Operators

The need to compare two values is a common operation in Java programs. We use comparison operators to perform these comparisons. Table 1.5 defines those operators with examples.

Operator

Comparison Operation

Example

Equal to

num1 == num2

num1 != num2

num1 > num2

num1 >= num2

Less than or equal to

num1 <= num2

Table 1.5: Java Comparison Operators

As noted in Table 1.5, the equal to comparison operator uses double equal signs (==). It is important to remember that when we use a single equal sign (=), it is assigning a value as we have done earlier in this chapter and is referred to as the assignment operator.

Logical operators allow us to test for true and false values. Table 1.6 defines those operators with examples.

Operator

Description

Example

&&

Returns true if both statements are true

!(num1 > num2 && num3 > num4)

Table 1.6: Java Logical Operators

Control Flow Statements

We do not always want all our code executed in a linear fashion; sometimes we only want sections of our code to run if certain conditions exist. That is where control flow statements come in. These take the form of condition statements or loops. Let us look at examples of both.

If-Else Statements

The if-else statement is a condition statement. Here is a simple example.

int age = 16;

if (age >= 18) {

System.out.println("You are old enough for this ride.");

} else {

System.out.println("You are not old enough for this ride.");

}

In the preceding code, if the condition is true, then the code within the if block will run. If the condition is false, the code within the else block will run.

Switch Statement

The switch statement is another condition statement and allows us to execute different code based on the value of a variable. Here is a simple example.

int jersey = 8;

switch (jersey) {

case 8:

System.out.println("Kobe's original jersey.");

break;

case 24:

System.out.println("Kobie's newest jersey.");

break;

case 32:

System.out.println("Magic's jersey.");

break;

default:

System.out.println("Jersey not found.");

break;

}

In the preceding code, the switch statement checks the value of the jersey variable and executes the corresponding case. The break statement keyword prevents the next case from executing.

Loops

Loops allow us to repeat a block of code multiple times. There are three types of loops in Java: for loop, while loop, and the do-while loop. Let us examine examples of each loop type.

The for loop executes a block of code a fixed number of times. Here is an example.

for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {

System.out.println(i);

}

This loop runs from i = 0 to i = 2, printing each value. The i++ increments the value of i each pass through the loop. Here is the output:

0

1

2

The while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition is true. Here is an example.

int j = 0;

while (j < 3) {

System.out.println(j);

j++;

}

Here is the output:

0

1

2

The do-while loop executes the code block at least once, and then continues based on the condition. This is a useful loop if you do not know if the condition will evaluate as true and you want the loop to run at least once. Here is an example.

int k = 0;

do {

System.out.println(k);

k++;

} while (k < 3);

Here is the output:

0

1

2

The condition statement and loop statement examples are in the Control.java file available in this book’s corresponding code repository.

Loops will be covered in greater detail in Chapter 2, Variables, Data Types, Operators, and Control Structures.

Book Long Project

This book features a book-long project that we will build throughout the first 19 chapters, progressively adding functionality in each chapter. Our application is an online Learning Management System (LMS) that allows instructors to create courses, manage content, track student progress, and provide assessments. Students can enroll in courses, access learning materials, submit assignments, and receive feedback.

In this chapter, we will kick off our application develop for our LMS application, which we will title Student Learning Access Platform (SLAP). Our objective in this chapter is to establish the project structure and lay foundational groundwork for further development. We will focus on setting up the environment and creating a simple, text-based interface for the SLAP LMS, which we will build upon in subsequent chapters.

Our first task is to initialize our project. Perform these actions:

  1. Create a new Java project in your IDE for the SLAP LMS.
  2. Set up the basic project directory structure. For now, a single folder is fine. We will expand on this in subsequent chapters.

Next, we need to create our main class. Perform these actions:

  1. Write the SLAPApp main class. It will be the entry point for our application, from which we will manage the application’s flow.

  2. Within the SLAPApp class, add a main() method that prints a welcome message to users. Here is an example:

    public class SLAPApp {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

    System.out.println("Welcome to the SLAP LMS!");

    }

    }

  3. Run the program to ensure it works.

Now we can create a simple text-based menu system within the SLAPApp class. This menu will present users with basic options such as "View Courses" or "Exit" (for now, these options will not have functionality, but we will implement them in future chapters). The structure might look like this:

public class SLAPApp {

public static void main(String[] args) {

System.out.println("Welcome to the SLAP LMS!");

System.out.println("1. View Courses");

System.out.println("2. Exit");

}

}

That is all we need to do with our SLAP LMS in this chapter. We will start expanding our Java application in the next chapter.

Conclusion

This chapter was designed to introduce you to the vast Java ecosystem and give you some familiarity with the inner workings of the language. We explored Java’s importance to modern software development and highlighted its portable, secure, and object-oriented nature. You had the opportunity to set up and test your development environment using the Java Developer Kit (JDK) and Visual Studio Code. We covered basic Java syntax, structure, control structures, and operators. The information provided in this first chapter was intended to serve as a foundation for the chapters that follow.

In the next chapter, we will look deeper into variables, data types, and structures that give us control over our Java program’s execution. These are fundamental building blocks of Java that build on the information you were exposed to in the first chapter.

Points to Remember

  • A constant in Java is declared using the final keyword and cannot be changed once initialized.
  • Arithmetic operators in Java include +, -, *, /, and % (modulus), which are used to perform basic mathematical operations.
  • A class in Java is a blueprint for creating objects, and every Java program must have at least one class.
  • Comments in Java can be single-line (//), multi-line (/* … */), or Javadoc (/** … */), and are used to document code and improve readability.
  • Control flow statements such as if-else, switch, and loops (for, while, do-while) allow for decision-making and repeating blocks of code based on conditions.
  • Garbage collection is a key feature of Java, allowing the JVM to automatically reclaim memory by removing objects that are no longer needed.
  • In Java, the main() method is the entry point of every program. It is declared as public static void main(String[] args).
  • Integrated Development Environments (IDEs), such as Visual Studio Code, streamline the development process by providing tools for writing, debugging, and running Java programs.
  • Java is a platform-independent language, allowing you to write code once and run it anywhere the JVM is available.
  • Java uses primitive data types such as int, double, char, boolean, byte, short, long, and float to represent basic values.
  • Logical operators in Java include && (AND), || (OR), and ! (NOT), which are used to evaluate boolean expressions.
  • Multithreading allows Java programs to execute multiple threads concurrently, improving efficiency and performance on modern systems.
  • Non-primitive data types in Java include objects such as String and arrays, which store more complex data.
  • The System.out.println() method in Java prints output to the console and is commonly used for displaying messages.
  • The switch statement in Java allows you to choose between multiple paths of execution based on the value of a variable.
  • The while loop in Java continues executing a block of code as long as a specified condition remains true.
  • Variables in Java store data and must be declared with a specific type, such as int, double, or String.
  • Writing a Java program requires compiling the .java source file into bytecode using the Java compiler (javac), which is then executed by the JVM.
  • The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is responsible for executing bytecode, managing memory, and providing platform independence.
  • The for loop is used to repeat a block of code a specific number of times.
  • The do-while loop in Java ensures that the loop body executes at least once before the condition is evaluated.
  • The if-else statement is a fundamental control structure in Java, allowing you to execute code based on whether a condition is true or false.

Multiple-Choice Questions

  1. What is the Java Virtual Machine’s role?
    1. Compiles Java source code into bytecode
    2. Executes Java bytecode and provides platform independence
    3. Manages the Java development environment
    4. Provides libraries for Java application development
  2. Which of the following is a primitive data type in Java?
    1. String
    2. Array
    3. int
    4. List
  3. Which of the following control structures is used to execute a block of code a specific number of times?
    1. if-else
    2. while loop
    3. do-while loop
    4. for loop
  4. What is the correct way to declare a constant in Java?
    1. const int PI = 3.14;
    2. final double PI = 3.14159;
    3. static int PI = 3.14;
    4. const double PI = 3.14.159;
  5. Which of the following is not a key feature of Java?
    1. Platform independence
    2. Object-oriented
    3. Manual memory management
    4. Multithreading support

Answers

  1. b
  2. c
  3. d
  4. b
  5. c

Key Terms

  • Arithmetic Operators: Operators used to perform mathematical operations, such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
  • Bytecode: The intermediate representation of Java code that is executed by the JVM.
  • Class: A blueprint for creating objects in Java; it defines properties and behaviors for the objects.
  • Control Flow Statements: Statements that allow you to dictate the flow of program execution, such as if-else, switch, and loops.
  • Data Types: The classification of data in Java, which defines the type of values a variable can hold, such as int and double.
  • Final Keyword: A modifier used to declare constants in Java; once initialized, its value cannot be changed.
  • For Loop: A control structure used to execute a block of code a specific number of times.
  • Garbage Collection: The automatic memory management process in Java where the JVM reclaims memory occupied by unused objects.
  • IDE (Integrated Development Environment): A software tool that provides comprehensive functionality for writing, testing, and debugging code.
  • If-Else Statement: A control structure that executes certain blocks of code based on whether a condition is true or false.
  • Java Development Kit (JDK): A software development environment used for developing Java applications, containing tools such as the compiler and the JVM.
  • Java Runtime Environment (JRE): A component of the JDK that allows Java programs to run, containing the JVM and class libraries.
  • Java Virtual Machine (JVM): A virtual machine that executes Java bytecode and provides platform independence.
  • Logical Operators: Operators used in boolean logic, such as AND (&&), OR (||), and NOT (!).
  • Main Method: The entry point of every Java application.
  • Multithreading: A feature in Java that allows concurrent execution of multiple threads, improving performance in multi-core systems.
  • Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): A programming paradigm based on the concept of objects that contain both data and methods.
  • Operators: Symbols used in Java to perform operations on variables and values, such as arithmetic and comparison.
  • Primitive Data Types: Basic data types in Java that store simple values, including int, double, and char.
  • Switch Statement: A control structure that allows multiple possible execution paths based on the value of a variable.
  • Variable: A storage location in a program that holds a value, which can change during program execution.
  • While Loop: A control structure that repeatedly executes a block of code as long as a specified condition remains true.
  • Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA): Java’s philosophy that enables the same code to run on any platform with a compatible JVM.
