CHAPTER 3

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Basics

Introduction

This chapter is an introduction to Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), a fundamental paradigm in modern software development. It allows programmers to create modular, reusable, and maintainable code by organizing software into objects that represent real-world entities. This chapter examines the core concepts of OOP, including how to define and use classes and objects, the building blocks of Java applications. The chapter explores how constructors are used to initialize objects, how inheritance allows us to extend existing functionality, and how polymorphism and method overriding provide flexibility in handling different types of objects. Encapsulation and abstraction, two critical OOP principles, will be explained in detail, demonstrating how they can help us manage code complexity and improve code security and clarity.

Once you fully grasp these foundational principles, you should be able to design and develop complex and well-structured Java applications.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to understand the core principles of Object-Oriented Programming and its importance in Java development. You will learn to define and use classes and objects to structure your Java programs, and create and utilize constructors to initialize objects, including the concept of constructor overloading. Furthermore, you will be able to apply inheritance to create hierarchical relationships between classes and utilize the super keyword, as well as explain and implement polymorphism, including method overriding, to enhance program flexibility. The chapter will also equip you to understand and implement encapsulation using access modifiers to protect data, and grasp the concept of abstraction to design abstract classes that provide a framework for future classes.

Structure

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

  • Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming
  • Defining and Using Classes and Objects
  • Constructors and Overloading
  • Inheritance and the Super Keyword
  • Polymorphism and Method Overriding
  • Encapsulation and Access Modifiers
  • Abstraction and Abstract Classes

Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm which, as the name suggests, centers around the concept of objects. Objects represent real-world entities or abstract concepts within a software system. Every object is a self-contained unit that contains both data (attributes) and behaviors (methods/functions) that manipulate the data. OOP allows us to break down complex software systems into component parts. This makes it easier and faster to develop, maintain, and scale.

OOP is not unique to Java, but it is especially important to Java because Java was built from the beginning as an OOP language. The result is a language that allows us to fully exploit OOP concepts such as modularity and reusability. Our programs are a collection of objects that interact with one another.

Here are four primary reasons why Java developers embrace OOP:

  • Modularity: Each object we create is a separate class (we will explore what that is in the next section) in our system. This means that each class can be developed, tested, maintained, and deployed independent of each other. This supports a modular software development schema which is a hallmark of modern Java development.
  • Reusability: Once we create a class, we can use it throughout our program as well as other applications. Knowing that our classes are likely to be used elsewhere underscores the importance of adhering to best practices, standards, and in-code documentation.
  • Scalability: OOP inherently supports overall application scalability. As our applications grow in complexity and use, we can adapt our code base one class at a time, instead of having to recode our entire program.
  • Maintainability: Modular code and OOP structures are easier to debug, test, and maintain. This is due to their focused design and smaller code base.

Now, let us briefly look at the four key principles of OOP programming. Each of these principles will be covered in greater detail later in this chapter.

  • Encapsulation: This important principle is the bundling of variables (data), and the methods (functions) that are used to manipulate that data, into one entity. That entity is a class. Classes in Java are a single file, and their encapsulation protects its data from modification by external entities. As you will see in the next section, we use access modifiers such as public and private.
  • Inheritance: Inheritance allows classes to inherit properties and methods from another class. This permits the reuse of common functionality among classes that have parent/child relationships. This is a key principle of OOP and is covered in detail later in this chapter.
  • Polymorphism: This concept can be somewhat difficult to grasp, and we will cover it in its own section later in this chapter. For now, you should know that polymorphism allows us to treat objects as instances of their parent class, even when they are instances of a subclass. This can result in dynamic and flexible code and enable us to write more generalized code that can be widely used. Again, we will cover this in greater detail later.
  • Abstraction: The fourth key OOP principle is abstraction, which allows us to simplify complex systems by modeling them based on key characteristics. We can create abstract classes to define the structure of our application without having to reveal any implementation details. This approach allows us to more easily manage complexity. We will look at this in depth later in the chapter.

Java makes it easy for us to implement OOP, so it is important for us to fully understand classes and the four key principles of encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. The rest of this chapter focuses on those concepts.

Defining and Using Classes and Objects

Objects and classes are the primary components of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). We previously established that everything in Java is an object. Classes are the blueprints for creating those objects. In fact, objects are instances of a class. We can consider classes to be blueprints or templates for objects. They define associated attributes (the data) and behaviors (the methods) that all objects of the class will have.

Let us look at the classic example of vehicles. Attributes for a vehicle, applicable to every vehicle, might include type, make, model, year, and more. Here is how we would define this as a class:

public class Vehicle {

// Attributes (fields)

String type;

String make;

String model;

int year;

// Constructor

public Vehicle(String type, String make, String model, int year) {

this.type = type;

this.make = make;

this.model = model;

this.year = year;

}

// Method (behavior)

public void displayAttributes() {

System.out.println("Type: " + type + ", Make: " + make + ", Model: " + model + ", Year: " + year);

}

}

Reviewing the preceding code, the Vehicle class has four attributes: type, make, model, and year. It also has a constructor that is used to initialize these attributes. The class also has one method, displayAttributes(), which outputs the attribute values for the specific instance.

Next, let us look at how to create an instance of a class. Remember, that classes are blueprints or templates, they do not contain any data. When we create an instance of a class, we are creating an object and assigning values. The process involves using Java’s new keyword. Here is an example:

public class Manufacturing {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// Creating an object of the Car class

Vehicle myVehicle = new Vehicle("Truck", "Ford", "F150 Limited", 2017);

// Accessing the object's method

myVehicle.displayAttributes();

}

}

The output of this is provided as follows:

Type: Truck, Make: Ford, Model: F150 Limited, Year: 2017

We successfully used the new keyword to create an object named myVehicle, of the Vehicle class. The class constructor initialized the attributes (type, make, model, and year). Our example also demonstrated use of the displayAttributes() method.

Let us take a closer look at class components and creating and using objects in the sections that follow.

Class Components

There are three primary components of a class: fields, methods, and constructors. You gained exposure to these components in the previous section; now it is time to dive a little deeper into them.

Fields

Fields are the variables that hold the state of an object. They are also referred to as properties and attributes. In our Vehicle class example, the fields are type, make, model, and year. Fields can be any data type such as primary types (for example, int), Strings, arrays, and even custom classes.

There are several different ways to initialize a field. First, we directly assign them in the class definition, as follows:

String type = "Truck";

We can also use a constructor as we did in our Manufacturing.java example using the new keyword.

In Chapter 4, Methods and Functions, we will examine additional approaches to initializing fields.

Methods

Methods define what actions can be performed by objects (instances) of a class. They typically execute operations on the object’s fields or otherwise make use of the data stored in fields. In addition to performing actions, methods can return values. For example, we might have an initiateDiagnostics() method as part of our Vehicle class that returns diagnostic results to the user.

We will explore this in greater detail in Chapter 4, Methods and Functions.

Constructors

Constructors are a special method that is automatically called when an object is instantiated. They are used to initialize an object’s fields. As you saw in our earlier example with the Vehicle class, the constructor has the same name as the class and there is no return type. Constructors use Java’s this keyword to refer to the current object’s instance variables. This is especially important when method parameters have the same name as instance variables.

Later in this chapter, we will look at additional options for using constructors. For now, it is important that you understand the following:

  • Constructors have the same name of the class.
  • Constructors use Java’s this keyword for contextual referencing.
  • Constructors are automatically invoked when a new instance of the class is instantiated.
  • Constructors do not have a return value.

Creating and Using objects

In Java, we use the following syntax to create an object from a class:

ClassName objectName = new ClassName(parameters);

Examining this syntax, ClassName is the name of the class that we are creating the object from; objectName is the name we assign to the object; new is the keyword that creates the object in memory; and parameters are the values we pass to the constructor.

An example from our Manufacturing.java application is as follows:

Vehicle myVehicle = new Vehicle("Truck", "Ford", "F150 Limited", 2017);

Once our instance of the class is instantiated, we can access individual fields directly. For example, if we want to print the model of our myVehicle object, we could use this code:

System.out.println(myVehicle.model); // outputs F150 Limited

Compete Example

Let us look at a more complete, real-world example to demonstrate the definition and use of a class. The following example defines a RetirementAccount class and then uses it to create and manipulate retirement accounts for customers:

public class RetirementAccount {

// Fields

private String accountHolder;

private String accountNumber;

private double balance;

// Constructor

public RetirementAccount(String accountHolder, String accountNumber, double initialBalance) {

this.accountHolder = accountHolder;

this.accountNumber = accountNumber;

this.balance = initialBalance;

}

// Method to deposit money

public void deposit(double amount) {

if (amount > 0) {

balance += amount;

System.out.println("Deposit successful. New balance: " + balance);

} else {

System.out.println("Invalid deposit amount.");

}

}

// Method to withdraw money

public void withdraw(double amount) {

if (amount > 0 && amount <= balance) {

balance -= amount;

System.out.println("Withdrawal successful. Remaining balance: " + balance);

} else {

System.out.println("Invalid withdrawal amount or insufficient funds.");

}

}

// Method to display account information

public void displayAccountInfo() {

System.out.println("Account Holder: " + accountHolder);

System.out.println("Account Number: " + accountNumber);

System.out.println("Balance: " + balance);

}

}

As you review our RetirementAccount class, you see that we included fields (accountHolder, accountNumber, and balance) to store account information. We also created methods (deposit(), withdraw(), and displayAccountInfo()) so we can manipulate the account’s data.

To use this class, we will create an AccountManager class, as shown:

public class AccountManager {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// Creat a new RetirementAccount object

RetirementAccount account = new RetirementAccount("Neo", "UP0021319", 3000);

// Use the object's methods

account.displayAccountInfo();

account.deposit(900);

account.withdraw(120);

}

}

Here we instantiate an account object from the RetirementAccount class, passing it parameters for the accountHolder, accountNumber, and balance. We also make calls to the displayAccountInfo(), deposit(), and withdraw() class methods. The output of this code is as follows:

Account Holder: Neo

Account Number: UP0021319

Balance: 3000.0

Deposit successful. New balance: 3900.0

Withdrawal successful. Remaining balance: 3780.0

Classes and objects are core to the Java programming language. It is important to understand how to define and use classes and objects as you start writing your own Java applications.

Constructors and Overloading

We established that constructors are a special method used to initialize objects and that they are automatically called when a new instance of a class is created. This approach ensures that our object’s fields are properly initialized. Let us use a new example, to help solidify our understanding of constructors and learn how else they can be used. The example used in this section will be a company’s employee management application.

Defining our Constructor

Here is an initial implementation of our application, starting with an Employee class. This simple class contains two fields (name, age), a constructor, and a method to display information.

public class Employee {

// Fields

String name;

int age;

// Constructor

public Employee(String name, int age) {

this.name = name;

this.age = age;

}

// Method to display information

public void displayInfo() {

System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", Age: " + age);

}

}

When we create an Employee object, the constructor is called to initialize the fields. Here is how we can create a new Employee object:

public class EmployeeManagement {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// Create a new Employee object

Employee employee1 = new Employee("Trinity", 24);

// Use the displayInfo method

employee1.displayInfo();

}

}

The output of this program would be the following:

Name: Trinity, Age: 24

Overloading our Constructor

Java allows us to overload a constructor, referred to as constructor overloading. This allows us to define multiple constructors in a class, each with a unique parameter list. This can be useful when we want to create more flexibility in our object creation. Let us update our Employee class, adding an additional field and a second constructor. Here is our updated code:

public class Employee {

// Fields

String name;

int age;

String position;

// Constructor 1 - accepts name and age

public Employee(String name, int age) {

this.name = name;

this.age = age;

}

// Constructor 2 - accepts name, age, and position

public Employee(String name, int age, String position) {

this.name = name;

this.age = age;

this.position = position;

}

// Method to display information

public void displayInfo() {

System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", Age: " + age + ", Position: " + (position == null ? "Not identified" : position));

}

}

As you can see in our updated Employee class code, we have two constructors. The first one only accepts the name and age as parameters; the second constructor accepts the name, age, and position as parameters. Java is smart enough to know which constructor to use based on the parameters passed.

You will also notice that we updated our displayInfo() method so it can handle all objects created from the Employee class, regardless of which constructor was used.

Now, let us create two objects, one from each of the constructors by updating our EmployeeManagement.java application.

public class EmployeeManagement {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// Create a new Employee object with Constructor 1

Employee employee1 = new Employee("Trinity", 24);

employee1.displayInfo(); // Use the displayInfo method

// Create a new Employee object with Constructor 2

Employee employee2 = new Employee("Neo", 32, "The One");

employee2.displayInfo(); // Use the displayInfo method

}

}

Here is the output of that application:

Name: Trinity, Age: 24, Position: Not identified

Name: Neo, Age: 32, Position: The One

Constructor Chaining

In the previous section, we created constructors to provide flexibility in object creation. It resulted in duplicative code. Both constructors had these same lines of code:

this.name = name;

this.age = age;

That might not seem like a big deal but imagine if our objects had 30 fields and we had a dozen or two constructors. That would result in a lot of duplicate code. Java has an answer to this in the form of constructor chaining. This is a method that allows us to call one constructor from another within the same class. The this() keyword is used in its implementation. Let us update our Employee class to demonstrate this. The code is provided here, followed by an explanation:

public class Employee {

// Fields

String name;

int age;

String position;

// Constructor 1 - default constructor

public Employee() {

this("Not identified", 0); // calls Constructor 2 with default values

}

// Constructor 2 - accepts name and age

public Employee(String name, int age) {

this(name, age, "Not identified"); // calls Constructor 3 with default position

}

// Constructor 3 - accepts name, age, and position

public Employee(String name, int age, String position) {

this.name = name;

this.age = age;

this.position = position;

}

// Method to display information

public void displayInfo() {

System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", Age: " + age + ", Position: " + position);

}

}

Our updated code now has a default constructor (Employee()) that calls the second constructor with default values for name and age. The second constructor (Employee(String name, int age)) calls the third constructor with default values for position. This ensures that all constructors eventually lead to our most specific constructor, constructor 3 (Employee(String name, int age, String position)). Here is an updated EmployeeManagement.java application that uses the updated Employee class:

public class EmployeeManagement {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// use default constructor

Employee employee1 = new Employee();

employee1.displayInfo();

// use Constructor 2 with two parameters

Employee employee2 = new Employee("Trinity", 24);

employee2.displayInfo();

// use Constructor 3 with two parameters

Employee employee3 = new Employee("Neo", 32, "The One");

employee3.displayInfo();

}

}

Here is the output:

Name: Not identified, Age: 0, Position: Not identified

Name: Trinity, Age: 24, Position: Not identified

Name: Neo, Age: 32, Position: The One

As you can now appreciate, constructors play a critical role in object initialization. Constructor overloading provides us with object creation flexibility. When paired with the use of constructor chaining, we can reduce code duplication and improve our code’s readability and maintainability.

Inheritance and the Super Keyword

Inheritance is one of the four main principles of OOP. It allows new classes to inherit properties (fields) and behaviors (methods) from an existing class. In other words, a subclass or child class can inherit properties and behaviors from a superclass or parent class. The terms sub class and child class are interchangeable, just as superclass and parent class are. This is like how a human child can inherit traits and habits (properties and behaviors) from their parents and grandparents.

We implement inheritance in our Java programs because it facilitates natural hierarchical relationships, method overriding, and code reuse. In Java, we use the extends keyword to identify when a class is inheriting from another class.

Let us create a Dog superclass and Corgi subclass that extends Dog. Here is the superclass:

// Superclass

public class Dog {

String name;

String size;

// Constructor

public Dog(String name, String size) {

this.name = name;

this.size = size;

}

// Method to display dog details

public void displayInfo() {

System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", Size: " + size);

}

}

The Dog class is straightforward with two fields, a single constructor, and a display method. Now, let us look at the Corgi class, a child class to the parent Dog class.

public class Corgi extends Dog {

int age;

// Constructor

public Corgi(String name, String size, int age) {

super(name, size); // call to superclass constructor

this.age = age;

}

// Display method

public void displayInfo() {

super.displayInfo(); //call to superclass method

System.out.println("Age :" + age);

}

}

As you can see, our Corgi class is a subclass that extends Dog and adds age as an additional field.

A subclass automatically has access to all non-private fields and methods of the superclass it inherits from. As you have seen, subclasses can add new fields and methods specific to itself. In addition, we can override methods from the superclass to provide a different implementation.

Super keyword

We have already used the super keyword, and it is important that we fully understand what it is and how it can be used. The super keyword refers to the superclass of the current object. We can use this keyword to call the constructor of the superclass and to call a method from the superclass that has been overridden in the subclass.

We have already seen the super keyword used to call the constructor of the superclass in our Corgi class example.

super(name, size); // call to superclass constructor

In that same class, we demonstrated the use of the super keyword to call a method from the superclass.

super.displayInfo(); //call to superclass method

Access Modifiers and Inheritance

Inheritance is controlled by access modifiers, which are keywords that set the accessibility of classes, methods, and fields. If we mark a field or method with the public or protected access modifiers in the superclass, they can be accessed and inherited by subclasses. If we mark them as private, a subclass will not be able to directly access them. We can access these private components indirectly via getter/setter methods (covered in the Encapsulation and Access Modifiers section later in this chapter).

If we want to prevent a class from being inherited, we simply declare it as final. Here is an example:

public final class Passwords {

// class code goes here

}

We can also use the final keyword on methods to prevent them from being overridden in a subclass. Here is an example:

public final void displayPassword {

// method code goes here

}

Polymorphism and Method Overriding

Polymorphism is one of the four core OOP principles. It allows us to treat objects of different classes to be treated as instances of the same superclass. Polymorphism enables methods to be processed differently depending on the object that invokes them. This is true even if the method shares the same name across classes. Polymorphism can be difficult to grasp, so let us dive deeper into this concept.

Simply put, polymorphism allows an object to take on many forms. We can accomplish this with compile-time polymorphism using method overloading and with run-time polymorphism using method overriding. We will focus on run-time polymorphism which, in Java, is simply referred to as polymorphism.

Run-Time Polymorphism

Run-time polymorphism takes place when a method is called at run-time based on the object being referred to, instead of the method being called based on the type of reference. This gives us added flexibility in our method invocation. In Java, run-time polymorphism is primarily accomplished through method overriding. This type of polymorphism relies on the concepts of inheritance and method overriding that we covered earlier in this chapter. These concepts allow a subclass to provide its own implementation of a method that is already defined in the superclass.

Let us look at a simple example using code snippets (not completed code):

// Superclass

public class Animal {

public void sound() {

System.out.println("Animal utters a sound.");

}

}

// Subclass One

public class Cat extends Animal {

@Override

public void sound() {

System.out.println("Cat meows");

}

// Subclass Two

public class Horse extends Animal {

@Override

public void sound() {

System.out.println("Horse neighs");

}

}

In this example, Cat and Horse are subclasses of the Animal class and overrides the sound() method to provide more specific information. Even though the method names are the same, each subclass behaves differently when the sound() method is called.

Encapsulation and Access Modifiers

Encapsulation, a core OOP principle, involves bundling fields and methods into a class. With encapsulation, we can restrict direct access to some object components. This is a critical aspect of applications that deal with sensitive or personal data. Encapsulation allows an object to hide its internal state and control how its data is accessed and modified through methods. The access and modification of data is typically handled through methods commonly referred to as setters and getters.

Setters and getters are also referred to as accessor and mutator methods. They are methods that allow us to control access to an object’s fields. Getter methods (mutator methods) are used to retrieve the value of private or protected fields. Setter methods (accessor methods) are used to update the value.

By default, fields are typically made private, so access is restricted from outside the class. Setters and getters represent a safe method of exposing fields in a controlled manner. To demonstrate setters and getters, we will replicate our Vehicle class, creating a new Vehicle2 class. Our new class includes a setter and a getter for each field, as shown here:

public class Vehicle2 {

// Private attributes (fields)

private String type;

private String make;

private String model;

private int year;

// Constructor

public Vehicle2(String type, String make, String model, int year) {

this.type = type;

this.make = make;

this.model = model;

this.year = year;

}

// Getter for 'type'

public String getType() {

return type;

}

// Setter for 'type'

public void setType(String type) {

this.type = type;

}

// Getter for 'make'

public String getMake() {

return make;

}

// Setter for 'make'

public void setMake(String make) {

this.make = make;

}

// Getter for 'model'

public String getModel() {

return model;

}

// Setter for 'model'

public void setModel(String model) {

this.model = model;

}

// Getter for 'year'

public int getYear() {

return year;

}

// Setter for 'year'

public void setYear(int year) {

this.year = year;

}

// Method to display attributes

public void displayAttributes() {

System.out.println("Type: " + getType() + ", Make: " + getMake() + ", Model: " + getModel() + ", Year: " + getYear());

}

}

Benefits to using setters and getters include data hiding, consistency, flexibility, code readability, and maintainability. In addition, we can easily add validation for our setters, ensuring that only valid data is introduced to the system. For example, we might modify our setter for our year field, as shown here:

public void setYear(int year) {

if (year > 1886) { // Cars were invented in 1886

this.year = year;

} else {

System.out.println("Invalid year");

}

}

We can access setter and getter methods through use of the dot notation or changing. Here are examples:

myCar.setYear[2024]

System.out.println("Updated Year Data: " + myCar.getYear());

In this example, we use the setYear() method to update the value and getYear() to review it.

Abstraction and Abstract Classes

The fourth principle of OOP is abstraction. It involves simplifying complex systems by modeling classes in a way that hides their unnecessary details. The primary purpose of abstraction in Java is to allow developers to focus on what an object does, without concern for how it does it. The goal is to reduce system complexity, especially in large systems.

As an example, when we use a copying machine, we do not need to understand the inner workings of the machine; we just need to know how to use the buttons to copy a piece of paper. The complexity of how the copying machine works is abstracted away from the user.

Java lets us achieve abstraction through abstract classes and interfaces. We will look at abstract classes in this section and conquer interfaces in Chapter 4, Methods and Functions.

An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated on its own and is meant to serve as a base class for other classes. These classes provide a structure for its subclasses and may contain one or more methods that are declared abstract. An abstract method does not have an implementation in the abstract class and therefore, must be implemented by any subclass.

In addition to abstract methods, an abstract class can also have concrete methods. This type of method is fully implemented and can be inherited by subclasses.

A typical use case for abstract classes is when you want to define a common interface and share behaviors across multiple related classes, but the exact details of some behaviors need to be determined by the subclasses.

Here is the syntax for an abstract class:

abstract class Vehicle3 {

// Abstract method (no implementation)

public abstract void startWipers();

// Concrete method (with implementation)

public void displayType(String type) {

System.out.println("Vehicle Type: " + type);

}

}

Book Long Project

You should now have a firm understanding of OOP and should be ready to start transitioning the SLAP LMS from a system based on variables and arrays into a more structured and modular application. You are now tasked with defining the core components of the system as classes and start implementing some of the essential functionality using objects and methods. The goal is to implement the building blocks for making the LMS scalable and maintainable as we continue to expand its features.

This section details six tasks that you should complete to move your SLAP LMS project forward.

Define Core Components as Classes

In Chapter 2, Variables, Data Types, Operators, and Control Structures, you were asked to outline the main components (such as, Course, Student, and Instructor). Now it is time to implement them as Java classes.

For each component, define attributes (fields) and behaviors (methods). For example:

  • Course might have courseName, courseID, and maxStudents as attributes, and enrollStudent() as a method.
  • Student will have attributes such as studentName, studentID, and methods including viewCourses().

Here is a sample Course Class:

public class Course {

private String courseName;

private int courseID;

private int maxStudents;

// Constructor

public Course(String courseName, int courseID, int maxStudents) {

this.courseName = courseName;

this.courseID = courseID;

this.maxStudents = maxStudents;

}

// Method to display course details

public void displayCourseInfo() {

System.out.println("Course: " + courseName + ", ID: " + courseID + ", Max Students: " + maxStudents);

}

// Getter and Setter methods

public String getCourseName() {

return courseName;

}

public void setCourseName(String courseName) {

this.courseName = courseName;

}

}

Create Constructors and Methods

With each of your core classes created, you are ready to use constructors to initialize objects with data. For example, when a new Course object is created, the constructor will take parameters such as courseName and courseID to initialize the object’s fields.

Implement methods to perform actions. For example, a Course might include methods to enrollStudent() and listEnrolledStudents().

Implement Inheritance

For this step, you are to introduce inheritance by creating a parent class User, which will hold common attributes for Student and Instructor. Both Student and Instructor classes will inherit from User.

Here is sample code for the User class:

public class User {

protected String name;

protected int userID;

public User(String name, int userID) {

this.name = name;

this.userID = userID;

}

public void displayUserInfo() {

System.out.println("Name: " + name + ", User ID: " + userID);

}

}

Here is sample code for the Student class:

public class Student extends User {

public Student(String name, int userID) {

super(name, userID); // Calling the parent class constructor

}

public void enrollInCourse(Course course) {

System.out.println(name + " has enrolled in " + course.getCourseName());

}

}

Implement Encapsulation and Access Control

Apply encapsulation by keeping fields private and using getter and setter methods to access and modify them. This helps protect the data and ensures that only authorized methods can manipulate the state of objects.

Introduce access modifiers (private, protected, public) to control visibility and data protection within the LMS.

Implement Polymorphism and Method Overriding

Introduce polymorphism by allowing methods to behave differently depending on the object that calls them. For example, both Student and Instructor could override a displayUserInfo() method inherited from User to display customized information based on their role in the system.

Build a Simple Object-Oriented LMS Interaction

Update the basic text-based interface to incorporate the use of objects. For example, users can create new courses and students and view the details of these objects.

Example code for interacting with objects:

Course javaCourse = new Course("Java Basics", 101, 30);

javaCourse.displayCourseInfo();

Student neo = new Student("Neo", 1001);

neo.enrollInCourse(javaCourse);

Next Steps

In Chapter 4, Methods and Functions, you will be tasked to expand on methods and functions by implementing additional functionality for interacting with courses, students, and instructors. You will also be able to introduce method overloading and recursion to solve more complex problems in the LMS.

Conclusion

This chapter explored the foundational concepts of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java, a powerful paradigm that allows for the creation of modular, reusable, and maintainable code. The chapter started with an examination of how to define and use classes and objects, which form the building blocks of Java applications. From there, we explored constructors and overloading with the goal of understanding how Java enables flexible object creation.

We covered inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, and abstraction, the four core principles of OOP. This coverage showcased how Java’s class hierarchy allows for the extension and dynamic object handling through method overriding. We say how encapsulation provides a way to protect an object’s internal state and control its exposure through access modifiers. The chapter’s coverage on abstraction illustrated how we can simplify complex systems by focusing on essential characteristics and behaviors.

In the next chapter, we will focus on methods and functions, which are essential for structuring code in Java. You can learn how to define, call, and pass parameters to methods, as well as how to return values. The chapter also covers method overloading and recursion, helping to provide you with the skills to write modular, efficient, and reusable code. In addition, interfaces will be covered.

Points to Remember

  • Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and are meant to serve as base classes for other classes.
  • Abstraction allows developers to focus on what an object does without needing to know how it does it.
  • Access modifiers in Java control the visibility of fields, methods, and classes.
  • Constructor chaining allows one constructor to call another within the same class using the this() keyword.
  • Constructors are used to initialize objects and are automatically called when a new instance of a class is created.
  • Encapsulation bundles fields and methods into a single class, protecting an object’s internal state by restricting direct access.
  • Fields, also known as attributes or properties, store the state of an object and can be initialized through constructors or directly within a class.
  • Getters (accessor methods) retrieve the value of private or protected fields, while setters (mutator methods) update their values.
  • Inheritance allows a subclass to inherit properties and behaviors from a superclass, promoting code reuse and maintainability.
  • Java’s super keyword refers to the superclass of the current object and can be used to call a superclass constructor or method.
  • Method overloading allows a class to have multiple constructors or methods with the same name but different parameter lists.
  • Method overriding enables a subclass to provide its own implementation of a method that is already defined in the superclass.
  • Objects are instances of classes, created using the new keyword, and store specific data for a class’s fields.
  • Polymorphism allows objects of different classes to be treated as instances of their superclass, enabling flexible and dynamic method invocation.
  • Setters and getters allow for controlled access to an object’s fields, ensuring data integrity and providing validation opportunities.
  • The extends keyword is used to implement inheritance in Java, allowing one class to inherit from another.
  • The four main OOP principles are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction.
  • The purpose of abstraction is to reduce system complexity by focusing on the essential features of objects while hiding the underlying details.
  • The this keyword refers to the current object and is used within constructors and methods to refer to instance variables.
  • Use of final on a class or method prevents inheritance or method overriding, respectively.
  • When creating objects from a class, fields are initialized either directly or through constructors.

Multiple-Choice Questions

  1. What is the primary purpose of encapsulation in Java?
    1. To allow multiple classes to inherit properties from one class.
    2. To protect the internal state of an object and control how its data is accessed and modified.
    3. To allow objects to be treated as instances of their parent class.
    4. To define the structure of an application without implementation details.
  2. Which keyword is used in Java to call the constructor of a superclass?
    1. this
    2. super
    3. extends
    4. final
  3. What does this() keyword do in constructor chaining?
    1. Refers to the superclass of the current object.
    2. Initializes static variables in a class.
    3. Calls another constructor within the same class.
    4. Makes a method abstract.
  4. In Java, what is the result of overriding a method in a subclass?
    1. The method in a subclass cannot be accessed.
    2. The method in the superclass is removed.
    3. The subclass provides its own implementation of the method.
    4. The method is automatically final in the subclass.
  5. Which of the following statements is true about abstract classes?
    1. They cannot contain any concrete methods.
    2. They cannot be directly instantiated.
    3. They must contain at least one abstract method.
    4. They cannot be extended by other classes.

Answers

  1. b
  2. b
  3. c
  4. c
  5. c

Questions

  1. How does encapsulation in Java improve the security and maintainability of code in real-world applications? Share a scenario that demonstrates how failing to use encapsulation could cause issues.
  2. Compare and contrast inheritance and polymorphism. How do they work together to allow for code flexibility and reuse in object-oriented programming?
  3. When would you choose to use an abstract class over an interface in Java? Provide examples of when abstraction would be beneficial in software design.
  4. How does method overriding help achieve run-time polymorphism? Provide an example where this feature could be useful in a project.
  5. Discuss the significance of constructor overloading. How does constructor chaining reduce code duplication, and what are the benefits of this approach?
  6. In what scenarios would you use access modifiers such as private, protected, and public? How do access modifiers help enforce encapsulation and secure sensitive data?
  7. In the context of OOP, why is it important for developers to understand the difference between the this and super keywords? How do these keywords affect inheritance and method calling?
  8. How does abstraction help manage complexity in large-scale software systems?
  9. Java allows for both method overloading and method overriding. How do these concepts differ, and when would each be appropriate in designing software?
  10. How does the concept of polymorphism promote flexibility in handling different types of objects in Java? Discuss how this might help in maintaining a scalable software architecture as a project evolves.

Key Terms

  • Abstraction: The process of simplifying complex systems by focusing on essential features and hiding unnecessary details.
  • Abstract Class: A class that cannot be instantiated on its own and provides a framework for subclasses to implement specific behavior.
  • Access Modifiers: Keywords that control the visibility and accessibility of fields, methods, and classes (such as, private, public, protected).
  • Class: A blueprint for creating objects, defining the properties and behaviors that those objects will have.
  • Constructor: A special method in a class that is called when an object is instantiated, used to initialize the object’s fields.
  • Constructor Chaining: The process of calling one constructor from another within the same class to reduce code duplication.
  • Encapsulation: The bundling of data (fields) and methods (functions) into a class, to protect data from unauthorized access or modification.
  • Field: A variable declared within a class that holds data for the objects created from the class.
  • Getter: A method that retrieves the value of a private or protected field, also known as an accessor method.
  • Inheritance: The process by which a subclass acquires the properties and methods of a superclass, promoting code reuse.
  • Method: A function defined within a class that performs actions or manipulates the data in fields.
  • Method Overloading: The ability to define multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists within a class.
  • Method Overriding: The process of providing a new implementation of a method in a subclass that already exists in the superclass.
  • Object: An instance of a class that contains specific values for the fields defined in the class.
  • Polymorphism: The ability to treat objects of different classes as instances of their superclass, allowing for dynamic and flexible method calls.
  • Setter: A method that allows you to update the value of a private or protected field, also known as the mutator method.
  • Super: A keyword used in Java to refer to the superclass of the current object, often used to call superclass constructors or methods.
  • This: A keyword used in Java to refer to the current object’s instance variables, often used in constructors and methods.

  • Create a constructor to initialize these fields and a method displayBookDetails() that prints the book’s details.
  • In the main() method, create two Book objects with different values and call the displayBookDetails() method for each object.

  • Overload the constructor so that you can create a Student object with just name and id, and another with name, id, and grade.
  • In the main() method, create two student objects using the different constructors and display their information.

Exercise 3: Demonstrate Inheritance

Objective: Practice inheritance and calling superclass methods.

Activity: Accomplish the following:

  • Create a method displayInfo() to print the appliance’s details.
  • Then, create a subclass Refrigerator that extends Appliance and adds the field capacity.
  • Use the super keyword in the subclass constructor to call the superclass constructor.
  • Override the displayInfo() method in Refrigerator to include the capacity field.

  • Write getter and setter methods for each field.

  • Write a main() method that creates a BankAccount object, sets the fields using the setters, and retrieves the values using the getters to display the account information.

CHAPTER 4

Methods and Functions

Introduction

The terms method and function are often used interchangeably and technically speaking, Java does not have functions like some other programming languages do. The key differences between methods and functions are that methods, in Java, are always associated with a class or object and functions, generally speaking, are not bound to a class and can exist independently. Java does not allow standalone functions outside of classes, so technically, the concept of “function” in Java is equivalent to “method.” This is an important distinction to keep in mind as we progress through this chapter.

Methods play a central role in structuring Java applications by promoting modularity and reusability. This chapter explores the various aspects of defining, calling, and managing methods in Java, including method overloading and recursion. You can learn about the significance of the static keyword when applied to methods. The chapter also introduces interfaces, which allow developers to set rules for what a class should do, without needing to focus on how it will be done. Understanding interfaces can enhance your ability to create flexible and modular code by leveraging polymorphism and clean design principles.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to define and call methods in Java with various parameters and return types, and utilize method overloading to create multiple methods with the same name but different argument lists. You will also learn to implement recursive methods to solve problems that require repeated function calls, and apply the static keyword to methods, understanding its impact on object behavior. Furthermore, you will grasp the concept of interfaces, defining and implementing them to create modular and abstract program structures. Finally, you will differentiate between abstract classes and interfaces, applying each appropriately, and use interfaces to achieve polymorphism.

Structure

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

  • Defining Methods in Java
  • Calling Methods and Passing Arguments
  • Method Parameters and Return Types
  • Method Overloading
  • Method Overriding
  • Recursion and Recursive Methods
  • The static Keyword in Methods
  • Introduction to Interfaces
  • Book Long Project

Defining Methods in Java

We previously introduced methods and the important role they play in our OOP approach to Java programming. The basic concept is to break our code into small, manageable parts. Methods are finite blocks of code that perform a specific task. In this section, we will take a more in-depth look at how to define methods in Java.

Methods can take input parameters, perform operations, and return values. Here is the structure of a Java method:

returnType methodName(parameterList) {

// method body

}

Methods have four components, each of which is explained, followed by examples in the subsequent section.

  • Return Type: Identified in our preceding example as returnType. This specifies the data type of the value returned by the method. In the case that a method does not return a value, we use the null keyword.
  • Method Name: Identified in our preceding example as methodName. This is simply the name we give our method. Names should be self-descriptive and use camelCase, where the first word starts with a lowercase letter and subsequent words are capitalized.
  • Parameter List: Identified in our preceding example as parametersList. Methods can accept input values. When we do not need input values, we simply leave this component blank.
  • Method Body: Identified in our example as a commented line (// method body). The method body is where the method’s code is placed. This is where we implement our logic and program the method’s actions.

In the next section, we will look at how to call methods and pass arguments.

Calling Methods and Passing Arguments

Now that we know how to define a method in Java, we need to understand how to call the method and pass values, more formally referred to as arguments, to them. When we “call” a method, we are telling Java to execute the method’s code.

To call a method, we use the method’s name followed by a pair of open and close parentheses. If the method requires parameters, then we place those inside the parentheses; otherwise, we leave the parentheses empty. Here are two examples:

student.showID(); // no parameters passed

student.setID(33000319); // passes a parameter

Methods with No Arguments

Methods are housed within classes, so let us look at how the showID() method might look inside a class.

public class Student {

// Method definition

public void showID() {

System.out.println("Student ID: 33000319");

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

// Creating an instance of the class

Student student = new Student();

// Calling the showID method

student.showID();

}

}

In the preceding example, we defined a showID() method that outputs a student object’s ID value. We called the method by first creating an instance of the Student class, then called showID() using the instance. The method did not take any arguments.

Methods with One Argument

Now, let us update our code to implement the setID() method which takes one argument.

public class Student {

private int id;

// Method to set the student ID

public void setID(int newID) {

this.id = newID;

}

public void showID() {

System.out.println("Student ID: " + id);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Student student = new Student();

// Calling the setID method and passing an argument

student.setID(33000319);

// Calling showID to display the updated ID

student.showID();

}

}

In the preceding example, we defined the setID(int newID) method that takes one argument of type int. When we call setID(33000319), the value 33000319 is passed to the newID parameter, and the student’s ID is updated.

Methods with Multiple Arguments

We can also create methods to accept multiple arguments. When calling one of these methods, we simply put the arguments inside the parentheses separated by commas. Let us look at an example by writing a method that creates a new student recording using first name, last name, and student ID as arguments.

public class Student {

private String firstName;

private String lastName;

private int id;

// Method with multiple parameters

public void create(String fname, String lname, int studentID) {

this.firstName = fname;

this.lastName = lname;

this.id = studentID;

}

public void showID() {

System.out.println("Student: " + firstName + " " + lastName + ", ID: " + id);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Student student = new Student();

// Calling the create method and passing multiple arguments

student.create("Neo", "Anderson", 00001);

// Calling showID to display the student's information

student.showID();

}

}

In the preceding example, the create() method takes three arguments: String fname, String lname, and int studentID. When calling the method, we pass "Neo", "Anderson", and 00001. The method stores these values in the student’s fields, and showID() prints the student’s full name and ID.

When dealing with methods that require multiple arguments, it is important to pass them in the order outlined in the method’s definition. For example, if a method takes two arguments, a String followed by int, you must pass the arguments in that order. If you pass arguments in the incorrect order, you could experience a compile-time error, or data corruption.

Passing Arguments by Value

In Java, arguments are passed by value, which means a copy of the argument’s value is passed to the method. Therefore, any changes made to the parameters inside the method do not affect the original values outside the method. Let us look at an example:

public class Student2 {

private int id;

// Method to set the student ID

public void setID(int newID) {

newID = 99999; // This change only affects the local copy of newID

}

public void showID() {

System.out.println("Student ID: " + id);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

int studentID = 54321;

Student2 student = new Student2();

// Attempting to change the ID

student.setID(studentID);

System.out.println("Original ID: " + studentID); // Prints 54321

}

}

In the preceding example, although the setID method attempts to modify the newID parameter to 99999, the original studentID variable remains 54321 because the method received a copy of its value, not the actual variable.

Method Parameters and Return Types

In the previous section, we created examples of methods that did not accept parameters, methods that accept one parameter, and methods that accept multiple parameters. In this section, we will take a closer look at parameters and return values in methods. Parameters are inputs to the method and return values are the method’s output.

Method Parameters

At this point, you should be familiar with parameters. They often referred to as parameters, formal parameters, inputs, arguments, and actual parameters. Let us review definitions for each of these terms to understand their nuanced differences.

  • Parameters: These are variables used in a method’s signature. They define the type of data that the method expects to receive each time it is called. Parameters act as placeholders that hold the actual values being passed to the method.
  • Formal Parameters: These are the specific variables listed inside the parenthesis as part of the method’s definition. These parameters define the type and number of inputs the method accepts.
  • Inputs: This is a general term that refers to any data or values that a method works with. When we pass values to a method, that method is receiving input.
  • Arguments: These are the real values or variables that are passed to a method when it is called.
  • Actual Parameters: This is another term for arguments.

Certainly, the five terms defined above have similar meanings. In fact, parameter and formal parameter are often used interchangeably, so let us look at the subtle difference between them. Parameter is a general term that refers to any variable listed inside a method’s signature. It can refer to both the formal (in the method definition) and the actual values passed (arguments) when the method is called. Formal parameters refer to the variables defined in the method definition. An easy way to remember the difference is that the formal parameters are the variables as they appear in the method definition, and parameter is a general term that can refer to both the variables in the method signature (formal parameter), and the arguments passed when the method is called.

Method Parameter Types

In Java, we can create methods that accept a wide range of parameter types. This includes primitive data types (for example, int and double) as well as reference types (for example, arrays and objects). Let us look at some examples in the following code:

public class Staff {

private int id;

// Method with a primitive parameter (int)

public void setID(int newID) {

this.id = newID;

}

// Method with an object parameter (Staff)

public void copyID(Staff anotherStaffMember) {

this.id = anotherStaffMember.id;

}

public void showID() {

System.out.println("Staff ID: " + id);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Staff staff1 = new Staff();

Staff staff2 = new Staff();

staff1.setID(3330319);   // Passing a primitive value

staff2.copyID(staff1);  // Passing an object reference

staff2.showID();   // Outputs staff1's ID

}

}

In the preceding example code, the setID(int newID) method accepts a primitive parameter of type int. The copyID(Staff anotherStaffMember) method takes a reference parameter that accepts another Staff object.

Methods can also be written to accept multiple parameters. To create this, we include a data type for each parameter and separate them with commas. Here is an example:

public void create(String firstName, String lastName, int staffID) {

// Method body

}

Referring to the preceding example, the create() method accepts three parameters, two of them are type String and the third is an int. Whenever this method is called, values for each parameter must be included and be in the prescribed order.

Method Return Types

When creating methods, we can have them optionally return values. In the cases when a method does not return a value, we indicate that with Java’s void keyword as shown here:

public void showID() {

System.out.println("Staff ID: " + id);

}

This example shows how to write a method that returns a staff member’s ID.

public int getID() {

return this.id; // Returns the value of id

}

In this example, we used the return keyword to return the value of id. Our method definition denotes int as the return type.

Methods can also return objects. In our Staff example, we can create a method that returns a Staff object. Here is how we could do that:

public Staff createStaff(String firstName, String lastName, int staffID) {

Staff newStaff = new Staff();

newStaff.create(firstName, lastName, staffID);

return newStaff;

}

In this example, the createStaff() method returns a Staff object after initializing it with provided parameters. The calling code can then use the returned object, as shown in the following example:

public static void main(String[] args) {

Staff staff = createStaff("Neo", "Anderson", 00001);

staff.showID();  // Displays Neo's information

}

As a final note, when use void in the method definition to indicate the method does not return a value, the method does not require a return statement.

Method Overloading

Java allows us to use multiple methods with the same name but different parameters. This is referred to as method overloading. We can implement this feature to improve the clarity of our code, make our code more reusable, and allow our methods to handle different types or numbers of inputs. This implementation is accomplished without the need for unique method names for each type and number of inputs. Best of all, Java determines which version of the method to invoke based on the type, number, and order of the arguments passed to the method.

Method overloading occurs when two or more methods in the same class share the name but different in one or more of the ways detailed in Table 4.1.

Parameter Differentiator

Associated Rule

Different number

The methods must have a different number of parameters.

Different types

The methods must have different parameter data types.

Different order

The methods can have the same numbers of parameters and data types but be in a different order.

Table 4.1: Parameter Differentiators and Associated Rules for Method Overloading

The benefit of method overloading is three-fold:

  • Code Readability: Method overloading allows us to use the same method name. This makes it easier for us to read and understand our code.
  • Code Reusability: The alternative to method overloading is creating multiple methods with different names based on the types and number of parameters. Method overloading therefore reduces code duplication and increases the ease of reusing our code.
  • Code Maintainability: Code that uses consistent method names allows us to modify overloaded versions of methods as needed. This makes code maintenance easier and less prone for errors.

Let us look at an example of method overloading:

public class Staff2 {

// Method to create a staff record with just an ID

public void create(int staffID) {

System.out.println("Staff member created with ID: " + staffID);

}

// Overloaded method to create a staff record with ID and name

public void create(int staffID, String firstName) {

System.out.println("Staff member created with ID: " + staffID + " and Name: " + firstName);

}

// Overloaded method to create a staff record with ID, name, and age

public void create(int staffID, String firstName, int age) {

System.out.println("Staff member created with ID: " + staffID + ", Name: " + firstName + ", and Age: " + age);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Staff2 staff = new Staff2();

staff.create(1001);  // Calls the first method

staff.create(1002, "Trinity");  // Calls the second method

staff.create(1003, "Morpheus", 32);  // Calls the third method

}

}

In the preceding example, we implemented the create() method, which is overloaded three times, each time with a different number of parameters. We called the create() method three times from within the main() method with the following results:

  • We first called staff.create(1001) and the first version of the method was invoked since it only requires one parameter (staffID).
  • Next, we called staff.create(1002, "Trinity") and the second version was invoked since it takes both a staffID and a firstName.
  • The third version was invoked when we passed three arguments: staffID, firstName, and age.

Let’s look at one more method overloading example, this time with different data types. The following example extends our Staff example and creates a setID() method, overloading it based on input type.

public class Staff3 {

// Method to set the ID using an integer

public void setID(int staffID) {

System.out.println("Staff ID set to: " + staffID);

}

// Overloaded method to set the ID using a string

public void setID(String staffID) {

System.out.println("Staff ID set to: " + staffID);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Staff3 staff = new Staff3();

staff.setID(1001);  // Calls the method with an int parameter

staff.setID("SN102");  // Calls the method with a String parameter

}

}

In this example, setID(int staffID) handles integer IDs and setID(String staffID) handles string IDs. Java will use the appropriate method based on the data type used in the method call.

Method Overriding

Method overriding allows a subclass to have its own implementation of a method that is already defined in its superclass. This core OOP feature allows polymorphism, which we covered in Chapter 3, Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Basics. Method overriding allows a subclass to modify or extend the behavior of a method inherited from its parent class.

When we override a method, the subclass version is used, and the superclass version is ignored. This is true if the method call comes from a subclass object. Method overriding is implemented by defining a method in a subclass with the same name, return type, and parameters as the superclass method. When a subclass calls a method, it first checks to see if there is an overridden version (overloaded) and invokes that; otherwise, the superclass method will be used.

Let us look at an example of method overriding in the code following snippet:

class Person {

// Method in superclass

public void showDetails() {

System.out.println("Person details.");

}

}

class Executive extends Person {

// Overriding method in subclass

@Override

public void showDetails() {

System.out.println("Executive details: ID, Name, Age.");

}

}

public class Main {

public static void main(String[] args) {

// Creating an object of the subclass

Executive executive = new Executive();

// Calling the overridden method

executive.showDetails();  // Output: Executive details: ID, Name, Age.

}

}

In this example, the superclass Person has a method called showDetails(), which outputs "Person details." The subclass Executive overrides this method with its own version, which outputs more detailed information on the executive. When we called the executive.showDetails() method, the overridden method in Executive is used.

As you saw in our example, we used the @Override annotation to indicate that the method overrides a superclass method. While the @Override annotation is not required by Java, it is considered a best practice for readability, troubleshooting, and maintainability.

Let us conclude this section with a look at rules for method overriding.

  • The subclass method must have the same signature as the one in the superclass. This means the name, return type, and parameter list must be identical.
  • The subclass method cannot have a more restrictive access modifier than the superclass method. For example, if the superclass method includes the public access modifier, then superclass method cannot use protected or private.
  • The return type should be the same in the overridden method as in the superclass. Technically, it can be a subclass of the return type, referred to as a covariant return type. For most cases, you can simply use the same return type in your overridden methods as are used in the superclass methods.
  • The overriding method cannot throw additional or broader checked exceptions that the original method. We will cover exceptions in Chapter 5, File and Exception Handling.

Recursion and Recursive Methods

Recursion is an advanced programming concept of a method calling itself to solve a problem. A recursive method solves a small part of a problem and then calls itself to work on a smaller instance of the same problem until some condition is met. Recursion can be difficult to understand and is especially useful for large problems that can be broken down into similar, sub-problems. An example is traversing a tree structure or, as you will see in this section, calculating factorials.

There are two parts to a recursive method: a base case and a recursive case. The base case is a condition that, when met, causes the recursion to stop. This is important because we do not want to inadvertently create an indefinite recursive method. A recursive case, the second part of a recursive method, is the part where the method calls itself with a smaller input. Each call of the recursive case should get us closer to the base case.

Writing recursive methods can be tricky and it is important to ensure that with each recursive call, the problem gets smaller and closer to the base case. If we do not do this correctly, our recursive method could continue indefinitely and result in a stack overflow error. Let us look at an example recursive method that calculates the factorial of a number.

Factorial

The factorial of a number, a mathematical construct, is denoted as n! with "n" being the number. So, we would write 8! to indicate a factorial of 8. The result is the product of all positive integers less than or equal to n, or in our case, 8. This is how we define factorial recursion:

n! = n * (n-1)!

The base case would be 0! = 1. Let’s look at how to program this in Java.

public class Factorial {

// Recursive method to calculate factorial

public int factorial(int n) {

// Base case

if (n == 0) {

return 1;

}

// Recursive case

return n * factorial(n - 1);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Factorial fact = new Factorial();

int result = fact.factorial(8);  // Calling the recursive method

System.out.println("Factorial of 8 is: " + result);  // Output: 40320

}

}

In this example, the base case is when n equals 0, which will result 1 being returned. The recursive case calls factorial(n – 1), reducing the size of the problem by one with each successive call until it reaches the base case. We can trace the recursive method’s execution to better understand how it works. Here are the steps our recursive method took to calculate the factorial of 8.

Step

Method call

Return

1

factorial(8)

8 * factorial(7)

2

factorial(7)

7 * factorial(6)

3

factorial(6)

6 * factorial(5)

4

factorial(5)

5 * factorial(4)

5

factorial(4)

4 * factorial(3)

6

factorial(3)

3 * factorial(2)

7

factorial(2)

2 * factorial(1)

8

factorial(1)

1 * factorial(0)

9

factorial(0)

1

Table 4.2: Trace of Recursive Method that Calculates Factorial of 8

Once our recursive method reaches the base case, the recursion can start unwinding as the method returns values up the call stack, eventually calculating 8 * 7 * 6 * 5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 40320.

In computer science, recursion is usually taught using the factorial mathematical construct, as we just finished covering. The Fibonacci sequence is another classic example used to teach recursion. So, let’s look at that next.

Fibonacci Sequence

The Fibonacci sequence, named after the Italian mathematician Leonardo Fibonacci, is the sum of the two preceding terms. Here is how to define this with recursion when n > 1.

fibonacci(n) = fibonacci(n – 1) + Fibonacci(n – 2)

It is also important to realize that fibonacci(0) = 0 and fibonacci(1) = 1. These will become base cases for our recursive method. Here is how we would implement this in code:

public class Fibonacci {

// Recursive method to calculate Fibonacci number

public int fibonacci(int n) {

// Base cases

if (n == 0) {

return 0;

}

if (n == 1) {

return 1;

}

// Recursive case

return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Fibonacci fib = new Fibonacci();

int result = fib.fibonacci(8);  // Calling the recursive method

System.out.println("Fibonacci of 8 is: " + result);  // Result = 21

}

}

Our recursive case adds the result of the two preceding Fibonacci numbers, eventually calculating the result.

Final Thoughts on Recursion

There are advantages and disadvantages to using recursion. It can result in more elegant code, which is easier to read and maintain. A disadvantage can be that it is less efficient than using loops instead of recursion. This is especially the case when we are dealing with large datasets. Recursive methods lead to high memory usage because each recursive call adds a new frame to the call stack. Your program might experience a stack overflow error if you have a large dataset, or it takes many calls to get to the base case.

For example, calculating Fibonacci numbers recursively can become inefficient due to repeated calculations of the same values. In this case, it might be more efficient to use an iterative programming approach.

The static Keyword in Methods

To this point, all of our programming examples with a main() method included the static keyword. It is time to explore the importance of that keyword.

public static void main(String[] args) {

}

A method marked static belongs to the class rather than instances of the class. This means that static methods, like our example main() method, can be called without having to create an object of the class. This is an important distinction. Static methods do not have to be part of an instance of a class, as they are static to the class itself.

There are three important characteristics of static method to understand. The first characteristic of static methods is that they cannot access instance variables or non-static methods directly. This is because static methods belong to the class itself and not an object. These methods can only operate on static variables and other static methods. If we attempt to access non-static variables or methods from a static method, our code will not compile and result in a compile-time error.

The second characteristic of static methods is that they are class-level methods. These methods, often used for utility or as helper methods, are tied to the class itself. The final characteristic of static methods is that they can be invoked directly using the class name. This can simplify code when we are creating objects. Let us look at an example where we use Math, a Java utility class.

public class StaticExample {

public static void main(String[] args) {

int nbr = 25;

// Calling a static method from the Math class

double result = Math.sqrt(nbr);  // No need to create an object of Math class

System.out.println("Square root of " + nbr + " is: " + result);

}

}

There are three primary uses for static methods. First, they are typically used as utility methods. These methods perform a general task that do not depend on instance variables. Examples include our previous Math code, sorting arrays, and manipulating strings. A second use is when constants or static data are involved. As an example, if we have a method that returns a constant value, it is likely a good candidate to be a static method. The third primary use is for factory methods, which is a creational design pattern that you can read about in Chapter 18, Design Patterns in Java.

Introduction to Interfaces

As we conclude our discussion of methods, we recall that methods must reside in a class. They can also reside in an interface. Interfaces in Java is essentially a structural contract that classes adhere to by including specific methods. This abstraction promotes loose coupling, making it easier for us to extend our code and maintain it.

In this section, we will explore what interfaces are in Java, how to define and implement them, and their difference from abstract classes.

Defining and Implementing Interfaces

An interface is a collection of abstract methods. An abstract method is a method without a body and exist for classes to implement. When we implement an interface, a class must provide concrete implementations for all its methods. An interface can also contain default methods, static methods, and constant variables.

To define an interface, we simply use the interface keyword. Here is an example:

public interface Identifiable {

// Abstract method

int getID();

// Default method

default void showID(int id) {

System.out.println("ID: " + id);

}

}

As you can see in our example, the Identifiable interface contains getID(), an abstract method, and showID(int id), a default method. The getID() method must be implemented by any class that implements the Identifiable interface.

To implement an interface, we use the implements keyword and must provide concrete implementations for all abstract methods in the interface. As class can implement multiple interfaces. Here is an example how to implement an interface:

public class Employee implements Identifiable {

private int employeeID;

public Employee(int id) {

this.employeeID = id;

}

// Implementing the getID method

@Override

public int getID() {

return this.employeeID;

}

// Using the default method from the interface

public void displayID() {

showID(this.employeeID);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

Employee employee = new Employee(10005);

System.out.println("Employee ID: " + employee.getID());

employee.displayID();  // Uses default method from Identifiable

}

}

In our example, the Employee class implements the Identifiable interface by providing an implementation for the getID() method. The class is also able to use the showID() method because it is provided by the interface as a default method.

Interface Inheritance and Polymorphism

Interfaces support polymorphism because multiple classes can implement the same interface and objects of those classes can be treated as objects of the interface type. This empowers us to write reusable and more flexible code.

When we implement interfaces, we treat them as objects of different classes that implement the same interface in a uniform manner. Let’s look at an example.

First, here is a simple interface:

public interface Drivable {

void drive();

}

Next, is a Truck class that implements the Drivable interface.

public class Truck implements Drivable{

@Override

public void drive() {

System.out.println("The truck is driving.");

}

}

Now, let’s create another class that implements the same Drivable interface.

public class Bus implements Drivable {

@Override

public void drive() {

System.out.println("The bus is driving.");

}

}

Next, let’s create a class that uses the Truck and Bus classes.

public class Automobile {

public static void main(String[] args) {

Drivable truck = new Truck();

Drivable bus = new Bus();

// Polymorphic behavior

truck.drive();  // Output: The Truck is driving.

bus.drive();  // Output: The Bus is driving.

}

}

In our example, both Truck and Bus implement the Drivable interface. As you saw, we can use the interface type Drivable to refer to both objects. This demonstrates polymorphism. The correct drive() method is called based on the actual object type.

Interfaces can also inherit from other interfaces, just like classes can inherit from other classes, as explained in Chapter 3, Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Basics. To accomplish this, we simply use the extends keyword, as we do for classes.

Differences between Abstract Classes and Interfaces

Abstract classes and interfaces are useful concepts in Java. They both allow us to create abstract methods that implementing, and subclasses must provide. Table 4.3 provides key differences between abstract classes and interfaces.

Feature

Abstract Class

Interface

Access Modifiers

Any access modifier can be used.

All methods are implicitly public unless defined as default or static.

Constructors

Can have constructors.

Cannot have constructors; cannot be instantiated.

Fields

Can have instance variables.

Can have only static and final fields.

Methods

Can have both abstract and concrete methods.

Can have abstract methods, default methods, and static methods.

Multiple Inheritance

Classes can only extend one abstract class.

Classes can implement multiple interfaces.

Table 4.3: Differences between Abstract Classes and Interfaces

Use Cases

While both interfaces and abstract classes enable abstraction, interfaces focus solely on the behavior a class must implement, without prescribing how the behavior is carried out.

Abstract classes should be used when we want to share code and possible state among related classes. This is useful when the classes being extended have a close relationship and some common behavior.

Interfaces should be used when we want to define a structural contract that can be applied to any class, regardless of where it lies in the hierarchy. Interfaces are especially useful for specifying behavior that can be shared by unrelated classes. When we leverage interfaces, we can build more modular and scalable applications.

Book Long Project

This section extends the SLAP LMS by implementing methods that allow our application to perform more complex and reusable actions.
