By working on this project, you can practice defining methods with parameters, overload methods, and utilize static methods for utility purposes. Additionally, we will introduce interfaces to define the structure of components such as Course, Student, and Instructor, without focusing on their implementation yet. This prepares us for greater flexibility and modularity as the project progresses.

This section details six tasks that you should complete to move your SLAP LMS project forward.

Implementing Methods for Core Components

Using the classes created in Chapter 3, Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Basics, (Course, Student, and Instructor) define methods that perform specific tasks related to these objects. These methods should include actions enrolling a student in a course, setting course details, and displaying information.

The following are example methods, provided for illustrative purposes only. Please note that they are not complete; you are encouraged to build your own methods and modify these examples as needed.

public class Course {

private String courseName;

private int courseID;

private int maxStudents;

// Method to display course information

public void displayCourseInfo() {

System.out.println("Course Name: " + courseName);

System.out.println("Course ID: " + courseID);

System.out.println("Max Students: " + maxStudents);

}

// Method to enroll a student

public void enrollStudent(Student student) {

// Logic for enrolling a student in the course

System.out.println(student.getStudentName() + " enrolled in " + courseName);

}

}

Method Overloading

Introduce method overloading by creating multiple versions of a method, such as enrollStudent(). One version may accept a Student object as an argument, while another version may take a student name and ID as separate parameters.

An example of method overloading is provided as follows:

// Overloaded enrollStudent methods

public void enrollStudent(String studentName, int studentID) {

System.out.println(studentName + " (ID: " + studentID + ") enrolled in " + courseName);

}

Creating Utility Methods

Use static methods for utility functions that do not require object state. For instance, you can implement a static method in a Utility class to format data or handle general calculations.

An example static method is provided here:

public class Utility {

// Static method to format course names

public static String formatCourseName(String courseName) {

return courseName.toUpperCase();

}

}

Introducing Interfaces

Define interfaces for the core components of SLAP LMS. Interfaces will establish a structural contract for the behavior of classes without defining how the behavior will be implemented. For example, create an Enroll interface that declares methods for enrolling students in courses.

Here is an example interface for enrollment:

public interface Enroll {

void enrollStudent(Student student);

void displayEnrolledStudents();

}

Next, implement your interface in the Course class. Here is an example:

public class Course implements Enroll {

// Implementing the enrollStudent method from Enroll interface

@Override

public void enrollStudent(Student student) {

System.out.println("Enrolling " + student.getStudentName() + " in " + courseName);

}

@Override

public void displayEnrolledStudents() {

// Logic to display enrolled students

}

}

Organizing Methods

Start thinking about how methods can be organized for flexibility. For instance, methods for enrolling students or displaying course details should be adaptable as the LMS grows in complexity. Using interfaces allows multiple classes to implement the same methods, enabling polymorphic behavior. You should start mapping out your approach to keeping your code organized.

Method Overriding

While interfaces declare method contracts, the actual implementation of methods can vary across different classes. Use method overriding to allow subclasses such as OnlineCourse to override certain behaviors (such as enrolling students in an online-specific way).

Next Steps

In Chapter 5, File and Exception Handling, we will explore file handling and exception management to allow the SLAP LMS to save and retrieve data from external files. This will provide data persistence for our LMS. We will also enhance its error-handling capabilities.

Conclusion

This chapter explored the essential concepts of methods and functions in Java, which are fundamental building blocks for creating modern applications. The chapter showed how to define and call methods, as well as how to pass parameters and return values. We then looked at more advanced topics such as method overloading, which enables methods to handle different types or numbers of inputs while keeping the same name. The concept of method overriding was also introduced, allowing subclasses to provide their own implementation of a method inherited from a superclass, promoting polymorphism.

The chapter also covered recursion, a technique where methods call themselves to solve problems by breaking them down into smaller, simpler tasks. Emphasis was placed on the utility of recursion, alongside a warning that recursion must be used with care to avoid inefficiencies and errors such as stack overflows.

We introduced the static keyword, which defines methods that belong to the class itself, rather than to instances of the class. You had the opportunity to learn that static methods are useful for utility functions and other tasks that do not depend on object-specific data.

Finally, we covered interfaces, which allow you to define a structural contract for behavior that classes must implement. Interfaces promote loose coupling and enable polymorphism, making our code more flexible and scalable. We also discussed how interfaces differ from abstract classes and when to use each.

In the next chapter, we will look at how to perform file operations in Java, including reading from and writing to files. The chapter will introduce the concepts of file streams, serialization, and deserialization, providing practical examples of how to store and retrieve data. The chapter will introduce exception handling, a critical aspect of building robust Java applications. You can learn how to anticipate and manage errors using try-catch blocks, and how to propagate exceptions through the method stack. The chapter also covers creating custom exceptions, which allows for more precise error reporting and handling in complex applications. By the end of the chapter, you should be able to manage file input/output and exception handling effectively in your Java applications.

Points to Remember

  • Abstract classes can have both abstract and concrete methods, instance variables, and constructors.
  • Arguments are the actual values passed to a method when it is called.
  • Base cases in recursion define the stopping point of the recursion to prevent infinite recursion.
  • Constructor methods are allowed in abstract classes, but not in interfaces.
  • Default methods in interfaces allow classes to inherit method implementations without requiring overriding.
  • Every method in an interface is implicitly public, and fields in an interface are static and final.
  • Formal parameters are the variables listed in a method’s definition that act as placeholders for incoming arguments.
  • If a recursive method does not reduce the size of the problem toward the base case, it will likely lead to a stack overflow error.
  • Instance methods in Java are tied to an object of the class and can access instance variables and other non-static methods.
  • Interfaces define a structural contract that classes can implement, specifying behavior without dictating how it is achieved.
  • Methods that are declared static belong to the class itself and can be called without creating an object of the class.
  • Method overloading allows multiple methods with the same name, but different parameter lists to improve code clarity and reuse.
  • Method overriding allows subclasses to redefine inherited methods, providing class-specific behavior and promoting polymorphism.
  • Multiple interfaces can be implemented by a single class, allowing for more flexible behavior across various objects.
  • Parameters define the expected inputs of a method and can include both primitive data types and reference types like objects.
  • Recursive methods break down problems into smaller instances of the same problem until they reach a base case.
  • Static methods cannot access non-static instance variables or methods and are often used for utility functions.
  • The @Override annotation is used to explicitly indicate that a method is overriding a superclass method, improving readability and maintainability.
  • The factorial of a number is a common example used to demonstrate recursion.
  • The final keyword in Java is used in interfaces to declare constant values, which cannot be changed.
  • The static keyword allows methods to be called at the class level, without needing an instance of the class.
  • Using polymorphism with interfaces enables objects of different classes to be treated uniformly based on shared behavior.
  • Void methods do not return any value and are declared using the void return type.

Multiple-Choice Questions

  1. What is the primary difference between a method and a function in Java?
    1. Methods in Java are always associated with a class, while functions can exist independently.
    2. Functions in Java are used for performing mathematical operations, while methods are used for all other tasks.
    3. Methods and functions are interchangeable terms in Java.
    4. Method in Java cannot return values, while functions can.
  2. What does the static keyword signify when applied to a method?
    1. The method can only be called after creating an instance of the class.
    2. The method belongs to the class itself and can be called without creating an instance of the class.
    3. The method must return a value.
    4. The method can only access instance variables.
  3. Which of the following is true about method overloading?
    1. Overloaded methods must have different names.
    2. Overloaded methods must have different return types.
    3. Overloaded methods must have different numbers or types of parameters.
    4. Overloaded methods cannot exist in the same class.
  4. Which of the following is a key characteristic of recursion?
    1. The recursive method calls another method to solve the problem.
    2. A recursive method solves a smaller instance of the same problem with each call.
    3. Recursion is only used in mathematical operations.
    4. A recursive method must have more than one base case.
  5. What is the main difference between abstract classes and interfaces in Java?
    1. Abstract classes can only have abstract methods, while interfaces can have both abstract and concrete methods.
    2. Abstract classes can have instance variables and constructors, while interfaces cannot.
    3. Abstract classes can be implemented by multiple classes, while interfaces cannot.
    4. Interfaces allow inheritance, while abstract classes do not.

Answers

  1. a
  2. b
  3. c
  4. b
  5. b

Questions

  1. Why is method overloading an important feature in Java, and how does it improve code readability and maintainability? Share a scenario in which you would prefer method overloading instead of creating different method names.
  2. In your own words, explain the difference between method overriding and method overloading. Why do you think Java allows both features? How do they contribute to object-oriented programming principles?
  3. Recursion is a powerful tool but can also lead to inefficiencies, such as stack overflow errors. What are some real-world problems where recursion might be more appropriate than iteration? How would you handle the potential drawbacks of recursion in a large application?
  4. The static keyword is frequently used in Java, especially for utility methods. Why might a developer choose to make a method static? Share perceived downsides or limitations of using static methods in a class.
  5. Interfaces and abstract classes are both used for abstraction, but they serve different purposes in Java. Discuss a scenario where it would be more appropriate to use an interface rather than an abstract class. How does the flexibility of interfaces impact software design?
  6. In Java, arguments are passed by value, meaning that changes made to method parameters inside the method do not affect the original variables. How could this behavior influence the design of methods that work with objects? Share ways to work around this limitation.
  7. Polymorphism is a fundamental concept in object-oriented programming. How does the use of interfaces enable polymorphism in Java? Provide an example from the chapter or your own experience where polymorphism improved the flexibility of a program.
  8. Java allows a class to implement multiple interfaces, enabling it to adopt behavior from different sources. How does this feature compare to the single inheritance model of abstract classes? Share potential challenges or complications when a class implements several interfaces.
  9. The chapter introduced both default and abstract methods in interfaces. How do default methods in interfaces impact the design of future versions of Java libraries? What advantages or challenges do default methods introduce, especially when compared to fully abstract methods?
  10. Recursion can be used to solve problems like calculating the factorial of a number or finding Fibonacci sequences. What are some other examples of problems that can be solved using recursion? How would you decide when to use recursion versus an iterative approach in your own projects?

Key Terms

  • Abstract Class: A class that cannot be instantiated and is meant to be extended by subclasses. It can have both abstract methods (without implementation) and concrete methods (with implementation).
  • Access Modifier: A keyword in Java that specifies the visibility of classes, methods, and variables. Common access modifiers are public, private, and protected.
  • Actual Parameter: Another term for argument; the real value passed to a method when it is invoked.
  • Argument: The actual value that is passed to a method when it is called.
  • Base Case: In recursion, the condition that stops the recursion by returning a value without making a further recursive call.
  • Code Maintainability: The ease with which a codebase can be modified or extended without introducing errors.
  • Constructor: A special method in a class that is called when an object is instantiated, often used to initialize the object’s state.
  • Default Method: A method in an interface that has a default implementation, allowing classes to inherit method behavior without overriding it.
  • Formal Parameter: A variable used in the method definition that acts as a placeholder for the actual argument passed during method invocation.
  • Interface: A collection of abstract methods that classes can implement, defining a structural contract for behavior without dictating implementation.
  • Iteration: The repetition of a block of code using loops, in contrast to recursion.
  • Method: A block of code within a class that performs a specific task. In Java, methods must be defined inside classes.
  • Method Overloading: A feature in Java that allows multiple methods in the same class to have the same name, but with different parameter types or numbers.
  • Method Overriding: A feature in Java where a subclass provides its own implementation of a method that is already defined in its superclass.
  • Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): A programming paradigm based on the concept of objects, which can contain data and methods. Java is an object-oriented language.
  • Parameter: A variable in a method’s definition that specifies the type of input the method expects.
  • Polymorphism: An object-oriented programming concept where one method or object can take on multiple forms, allowing different classes to respond to the same method call.
  • Recursion: A programming technique where a method calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem, continuing until it reaches a base case.
  • Return Type: The data type of the value that a method returns. If the method does not return a value, its return type is void.
  • Stack Overflow: An error that occurs when a program runs out of stack space, often due to deep or infinite recursion.
  • Static Method: A method that belongs to the class itself rather than an instance of the class, allowing it to be called without creating an object.
  • Utility Method: A static method that performs a general, often reusable task, and does not rely on instance-specific data.

Exercises

Exercise 1: Overloading Methods

Objective: Understand method overloading by creating multiple methods with the same name but different parameters.

Activity: Write a Java class called Calculator that contains three overloaded methods called calculate(). Implement these guidelines:

  • The first method should take two integers and return their sum.
  • The second method should take two double values and return their product.
  • The third method should take three integers and return the average of those numbers.

Test each method in the main() function by creating instances of the Calculator class and calling the calculate() method with different sets of arguments.

Exercise 2: Implementing Recursive Methods

Objective: Learn to write and trace recursive methods by implementing a common mathematical function.

Activity: Write a Java program that defines a recursive method sumOfDigits(int n) that calculates the sum of the digits of a given integer n. For example, the sum of digits of 123 is 6 (1 + 2 + 3). Test the method with various input values, ensuring it returns the correct sum. Include a base case to stop recursion when the number has been reduced to a single digit. Be sure to provide ample in-code comments.

Exercise 3: Utilizing Static Methods

Objective: Practice writing and using static methods that do not rely on object-specific data.

Activity: Create a Java class called MathHelper that contains static methods for common mathematical operations: isPrime(int n), gcd(int a, int b), and factorial(int n). These methods should not rely on any instance variables. In your main() method, call these static methods directly from the class (without creating an instance) and test their functionality with different inputs.

Exercise 4: Implementing an Interface

Objective: Understand how to define and implement interfaces in Java.

Activity: Follow these steps to complete this exercise:

  1. Define an interface called Playable with two methods: start() and stop().
  2. Create two classes, MusicPlayer and VideoPlayer, that both implement the Playable interface. Each class should provide its own implementation for the start() and stop() methods, displaying appropriate messages.
  3. Write a main class that creates instances of both MusicPlayer and VideoPlayer, and call the start() and stop() methods on each.

Exercise 5: Exploring Method Overriding

Objective: Demonstrate the use of method overriding to customize inherited behavior in subclasses.

Activity: Follow these steps to complete this exercise:

  1. Create a superclass called Vehicle with a method fuelEfficiency() that prints a generic message.
  2. Create two subclasses, Car and Motorcycle, that override the fuelEfficiency() method to provide specific messages about the fuel efficiency of each vehicle.
  3. In your main() method, create instances of both Car and Motorcycle and call their fuelEfficiency() methods to demonstrate method overriding.

CHAPTER 5

File and Exception Handling

Introduction

This chapter explores two essential aspects of Java programming: file handling and exception handling. File handling is a fundamental skill that allows us to interact with external data sources by reading from and writing to files. We will explore how to work with text and binary files using Java’s file streams, and discuss the process of serialization and deserialization to efficiently store and retrieve complex data structures.

Exception handling is a critical component in developing reliable and robust applications. This chapter demonstrates how to use Java to detect and respond to runtime errors, ensuring that our programs can gracefully handle unexpected situations. From basic try-catch blocks to creating our own custom exceptions, this chapter presents the tools necessary to manage errors effectively and improve the resilience of our Java applications.

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to read from and write to text and binary files using Java, use file streams such as FileInputStream, FileOutputStream, BufferedReader, and BufferedWriter, and serialize and deserialize Java objects for efficient data storage and retrieval. You will also understand the Java exception handling framework and how exceptions are propagated, implement try, catch, and finally blocks to handle runtime errors, create, and throw custom exceptions for more precise error handling, and apply best practices for managing file operations and exceptions in Java.

Structure

In this chapter, the following topics will be covered:

  • Introduction to File Handling
  • Reading and Writing Text Files
  • Working with Binary Files
  • File Streams
  • Serialization and Deserialization
  • Understanding Exceptions in Java
  • Handling File-Related Exceptions
  • The try, catch, and finally Blocks
  • Throwing and Propagating Exceptions
  • Creating Custom Exceptions
  • Best Practices in Exception Handling

Introduction to File Handling

Many of the applications you write are apt to work with files. This could be in the form of creating, exporting, reading, listing, or other type of file manipulation. The benefit of using files in our application can be simply to hold configuration data or as advanced as providing the user the ability to store data for later retrieval. As you might expect, Java has a robust feature set to help us read, write, and otherwise work with files.

In Java, we can work with text files and binary files. Text files are those that are in human-readable format and easily opened with any word or text editor. Binary files are formatted differently and are computer readable. Binary file type examples include databases and images.

As you can read later in this chapter, Java includes a powerful set of classes to facilitate file operations to include FileReader and FileWriter. These classes are aptly named and provide the functionality for opening, reading, writing, and closing files. These are the basic file operations, but there is more. We can work with more complex data such as file streams using BufferedReader and BufferedWriter to help incorporate efficiency into our applications by buffering data during our application’s reading and writing operations.

An important part of working with files is the incorporation of error management. Here are some of the things we need to account for:

  • What if the file we are trying to open does not exist?
  • What if our application does not have permission to update a file?
  • What if the directory or file folder does not exist?
  • What if the file we are trying to save already exists?

You can probably think of additional scenarios specific to your applications. Fortunately, Java makes it relatively easy to handle these types of instances using exceptions. We will explore how to handle exceptions later in this chapter.

Reading and Writing Text Files

Let us explore the two most common text file operations: reading and writing. Developers almost always must content with files even if the application does not engage the user with the operations. Even game developers write code that works with text files. At a minimum, text files can be used for configurations, profiles, templates, and logs. It becomes clear that learning how to program read and write operations for text files is important for all Java developers.

Reading Text Files

The two primary methods of reading text files are with the FileReader class or the BufferedReader class. We will review both classes and include examples.

FileReader Class

The FileReader class is a good tool for basic text file reading. Although it lacks efficiency, it is sufficient for small files. Let us look at some implementation examples. This first example reads one character at a time and echoes it to the output window. As you can see, the FileReader class uses -1 to indicate the end of the file.

import java.io.*;

public class ReadOneChar {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

FileReader reader = new FileReader("Example1.txt");

int character;

while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {

System.out.print((char) character);

}

reader.close();

}

}

Take note that the FileReader class is part of the java.io package, so we need to include the import statement, as shown in the preceding code.

Now, let us look at a second example that uses the FileReader class to read one word at a time. This time, in addition to the FileReader class, we need to use the Scanner class.

import java.io.*;

import java.util.Scanner;

public class ReadOneWord {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

Scanner scanner = new Scanner(new File("Example1.txt"));

while (scanner.hasNext()) {

String word = scanner.next();

System.out.println(word);

}

scanner.close();

}

}

This example checks for one word at a time and continues as long as the Scanner’s hasNext() method returns true, signifying there is at least one word left in the file.

Let’s look at one more example; one that reads a text file one line at a time.

import java.io.*;

import java.util.Scanner;

public class ReadOneLine {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

FileReader fr = new FileReader("Example2.txt");

Scanner scanner = new Scanner(fr);

while (scanner.hasNextLine()) {

String line = scanner.nextLine();

System.out.println(line);

}

scanner.close();

fr.close();

}

}

This example reads one line of the file at a tie, putting it in the line variable and then echoing it to the screen. The process continues until the hasNextline() method returns false, indicating the last line was already processed.

Next, let’s look at these examples using the BufferedReader class.

BufferedReader Class

It is advisable to use the BufferedReader class, in conjunction with the FileReader class for larger files. This should increase the efficiency of your read/write operations. The BufferedReader class reads from a character input stream. It buffers characters for greater efficiency.

Our first example reads one character at a time.

import java.io.*;

public class ReadOneCharBuffered {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("Example1.txt"));

int character;

while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {

System.out.print((char) character);

}

reader.close();

}

}

This second example reads one word at a time.

import java.io.*;

public class ReadOneWordBuffered {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("Example1.txt"));

String line;

while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {

String[] words = line.split("\\s+");

for (String word : words) {

System.out.println(word);

}

}

reader.close();

}

}

Our final example reads one line at a time.

import java.io.*;

public class ReadOneLineBuffered {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("Example2.txt"));

String line;

while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {

System.out.println(line);

}

reader.close();

}

}

Note: In each of these examples, we included "throws IOException" as part of the main() method definition. You will see this in the examples for writing to files too. We will cover this later in the chapter.

Writing Text Files

We can use the FileWriter and the BufferedWriter classes to write to text files. Let’s examine examples of both.

FileWriter Class

We can use the FileWriter class for writing characters to a file. Let’s look at a simple example:

import java.io.*;

public class WriteToFile {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

FileWriter writer = new FileWriter("WriteExample1.txt");

writer.write("Hello, Java!\n");

writer.write("Java is the name of my Corgi puppy.");

writer.close();

}

}

In the preceding example, we write two lines to a new WriteExample1.txt file in the same directory or path that our program resides in. We can optionally include the path to the file inside the "WriteExample1.txt" string.

Also noteworthy, we included \n in our first string. This is known as an escape character; it signifies a new line.

BufferedWriter Class

We can rewrite our previous program using the BufferedWriter class for greater efficiency. This is most appropriate with large files.

import java.io.*;

public class WriteToFileBuffered {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

BufferedWriter writer = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("WriteExample2.txt"));

writer.write("Hello, Java!");

writer.newLine();

writer.write("Java is the name of my Corgi puppy.");

writer.close();

}

}

The difference between these two approaches (FileWriter and BufferedWriter) is subtle, but great efficiency can be had from using BufferedWriter in conjunction with FileWriter. Also, note that we did not use the \n escape character for a new line; instead, we used the newline() method. Both versions of the program result in the following being written to file:

Hello, Java!

Java is the name of my Corgi puppy.

Working with Binary Files

Binary files are not human readable and are commonly used for audio, images, and other objects. As you will see in this section’s examples, Java provides several classes to help us work with binary files.

Reading Binary Files

The following program uses Java’s FileInputStream class to read a binary file named Hello.bin. It reads the file byte by byte and prints each value to the screen.

import java.io.*;

public class BinaryReadingExample {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

FileInputStream inputStream = new FileInputStream("Hello.bin");

int byteData;

while ((byteData = inputStream.read()) != -1) {

System.out.print(byteData + " ");

}

inputStream.close();

}

}

Here is the output of the program:

72 101 108 108 111

As you can see, ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) values are output. The values equate to the letters H e l l o.

Writing Binary Files

To write to a binary file, we can use the FileOutputStream class. The following example writes the ASCII values of the letters H e l l o to a binary file named Example1.bin.

import java.io.*;

public class BinaryWritingExample1 {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

FileOutputStream outputStream = new FileOutputStream("Example1.bin");

outputStream.write(72);  //  the ASCII value for 'H'

outputStream.write(101); //  the ASCII value for 'e'

outputStream.write(108); //  the ASCII value for 'l'

outputStream.write(108); //  the ASCII value for 'l'

outputStream.write(111); //  the ASCII value for 'o'

outputStream.close();

}

}

Additional Options with Binary Data

Java has additional classes we can use with binary files. For example, we can use DataInputStream and DataOutputStream for reading and writing primitive data types in binary format.

File Streams

In Java, a file stream is a sequence of data that comes from or to a file. These streams are used to handle input and output operations. The streams of data can be transferred between systems, files, displays, and other sources. This is an efficient way to process data.

For input streams, we can use the FileReader, FileInputStream, and BufferedReader classes. Java has the FileWriter, FileOutputStream, and BufferedWriter classes for output streams. Here is a file stream example where the ASCII values for J, A, V, and A are output file named Example2.bin using FileOutputStream and then reads from that same file using FileInputStream, printing the results to the screen.

import java.io.*;

public class FileStreamExamples {

public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

// Writing data to a binary file

FileOutputStream outputStream = new FileOutputStream("Example2.bin");

outputStream.write(74); // ASCII value for 'J'

outputStream.write(65); // ASCII value for 'A'

outputStream.write(86); // ASCII value for 'V'

outputStream.write(65); // ASCII value for 'A'

outputStream.close();

// Reading data from the binary file

FileInputStream inputStream = new FileInputStream("Example2.bin");

int byteData;

while ((byteData = inputStream.read()) != -1) {

System.out.print((char) byteData + " ");

}

inputStream.close();

}

}

Streams are covered in greater detail in Chapter 6, Input/Output Streams.

Serialization and Deserialization

Java enables us to implement serialization, which is the conversion of any object into a byte stream, and deserialization, which restores the object back to its original state. Serialization is accomplished using the ObjectOutputStream class and Deserialization uses the ObjectInputStream class.

Serialization and deserialization empower us to perform advanced data exchange with relative ease. Here are the most common use cases for implementing serialization and deserialization:

  • Caching
  • Deep Copying
  • JavaBeans
  • Networking
  • Storing Objects

To better understand serialization, consider the action of saving an object’s complete state (for example, the object structure and values of variables) so we can store it in a file, send it over a network, or save it in memory for later use. The object is flattened into a sequence of bytes that can be written to disk or sent elsewhere; this is the process of serialization. Deserialization occurs when we reverse the process: it reads the byte sequence and reconstructs the object in memory, complete with its original attributes.

This is a powerful tool, especially when we use it recursively, resulting in all nested or referenced objects being included in the byte stream. Of course, only classes that implement the Serializable interface can be serialized. Furthermore, certain static fields are not preserved by default. Understanding these nuances can help you design object models that can be reliably saved and restored across different sessions or systems.

Understanding Exceptions in Java

Exceptions in Java are unexpected errors that arise during a program’s execution. These exceptions can result in a program crash, unexpected results, a poor user experience, and program flow interruption. Exceptions can be caused by division by zero, missing database connection, network problems, invalid user input and, for the context of this chapter, file not found errors.

The bad news is that we do not know if these errors will occur when our application runs. The good news is we can plan for them, should they occur. Java gives us the ability to test for them. We will discuss it later in this section. For now, let us look at code that will throw an exception.

public class ExceptionExample1 {

public static void main(String[] args) {

int nbrA = 10;

int nbrB = 0;

int result = nbrA / nbrB; // This throws an ArithmeticException

System.out.println("Result: " + result);

}

}

The preceding example attempts to divide by zero and results in an ArtihmeticException. This disrupts the program flow. The output is shown as follows:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero

at ExceptionExample1.main(ExceptionExample1.java:5)

If we coded the program as shown here, we already know that dividing by zero throws an exception. The problem is if we are accepting input from outside of our program such as from a user, file, database, stream, or other source. We will come back to this program later in this section and modify so it does not disrupt the flow of the program.

Exception Types

In Java, there are two main exception types: checked exceptions and unchecked exceptions. Checked exceptions are checked at compile-time, so we must explicitly handle them. Here are examples with self-descriptive names:

  • FileNotFoundException
  • IOException
  • SQLException

We can easily recover from this type of error. For example, review the following code to see how we handle an error when a file we are trying to read from is not found.

import java.io.*;

public class ExceptionExample2 {

public static void main(String[] args) {

try {

FileReader reader = new FileReader("thisFileDoesNotExist.txt");

} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {

System.out.println("File not found: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

}

Instead of an exception error message that we saw with our ExceptionExample1 program, we now gracefully handled the exception, resulting in the following output:

File not found: thisFileDoesNotExist.txt (No such file or directory)

The second type of exception is the unchecked exception. These are exceptions that are not checked when the application is compiled and can occur during runtime. Common examples include:

  • ArithmeticException
  • ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
  • NullPointerException

We demonstrated an ArthmeticException with our ExceptionExample1 program.

Importance of Handling Exceptions

In Java, exception handling is the art of programming our applications so they can handle runtime errors. Our goal is to ensure our program’s operation flow is not impacted by unexpected issues. It is like having a net when walking a tightrope. You do not plan to fall, but if you do your fall will be handled gracefully. This is our approach in Java, we want to gracefully handle any errors our application encounters at runtime.

We use the following listed keywords to handle our exceptions:

  • Try: A try block has the code that might throw an exception.
  • Catch: This block captures and handles the exception.
  • Finally: This block is executed whether or not an exception was thrown.
  • Throw: We can use this block to explicitly throw an exception.

Here are the top three reasons why we must handle exceptions in our programs:

  • Feedback: We can provide users with contextual and very specific feedback on the errors during runtime. This is preferable over system-generated generic error messages.
  • Recovery: We do not want our programs to crash when an error is encountered; rather, we want to gracefully recover from all errors during runtime. Consider the user experience of simply receiving a message such as ‘That file was not found, please try again’ compared to a system crash.
  • Stability: We want our programs to continue running when errors are encountered. Proper error handling helps us achieve that goal.

In the next section, we will implement these keywords.

Handling File-Related Exceptions

In the beginning of this chapter, we identified file operations as a common part of most Java applications. Those operations are also a potential source of runtime exceptions to include access issues, missing files, missing folder/directory, and more.

Before we start coding file-related exception handling, we need to consider three general practices:

  • Feedback: Provide the user with detailed and contextual feedback. Be specific and guide the user to overcome the error. For example, maybe they provided invalid input. In that case, tell them exactly what they did wrong and reiterate the input rules. Do not simply say, “Invalid input, try again” as that is insulting and not specific enough.
  • Fallback: In some cases, you can implement a fallback mechanism when an error is encountered. For example, if the user wants to open a file and the file does not exist, then you might create a new file with the same name or allow the user to select another file name or location.
  • Resources: Be mindful how resource intensive some file operations are. Configure your error handling so resources are not wasted.

Next, we will explore how to code file-related exception handling.

The try, catch, and finally Blocks

As previously stated, file operations are prone to exceptions, and we must handle those exceptions in the programs we write. Fortunately, Java provides us with try, catch, and finally blocks to handle these exceptions. This section explains the syntax for these blocks and provides implementation examples.

Syntax and Structure

Here is the syntax and structure of Java’s try, catch, and finally blocks:

try {

// This is the code that might throw an exception

} catch (ExceptionType e) {

// This code handles the exception

} finally {

// This code always execution, regardless of whether an exception occurred

}

Let us look at a simple example by rewriting our ReadOneChar.java program we created earlier in this chapter.

import java.io.*;

public class ReadOneCharWithErrorHandling {

public static void main(String[] args) {

FileReader reader = null;

try {

reader = new FileReader("Example1.txt");

int character;

while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {

System.out.print((char) character);

}

} catch (IOException e) {

System.err.println("An error occurred: " + e.getMessage());

} finally {

if (reader != null) {

try {

reader.close();

} catch (IOException e) {

System.err.println("Failed to close the reader: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

}

}

}

This code checks if the file exists and if it does not, an error is displayed to the user. The application also closes the reader to be a good shepherd of system resources.

Writing Multiple Catch Blocks

We can catch multiple exceptions in one set of try-catch blocks. Here is an example:

import java.io.*;

public class MultipleCatches {

public static void main(String[] args) {

try {

FileReader reader = new FileReader("NoWhereToBeFound.txt");

int character = reader.read();

int result = 10 / 0; // This will throw an ArithmeticException

} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {

System.out.println("File not found: " + e.getMessage());

} catch (ArithmeticException e) {

System.out.println("Cannot divide by zero: " + e.getMessage());

} catch (IOException e) {

System.out.println("I/O error occurred: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

}

As you can see, we can handle different types of exceptions separately in the same try-catch structure. In our example code, each type of exception is handled by a separate catch block.

Ensuring Resource Cleanup

It is important that we cleanup our resources to include closing network connections, closing files, and closing database connections. The finally block, because it is guaranteed to execute, is commonly used for resource cleanup. Here is an example:

import java.io.*;

public class CleanupExample {

public static void main(String[] args) {

FileReader reader = null;

try {

reader = new FileReader("NoWhereToBeFound.txt");

// Perform file operations

} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {

System.out.println("File not found: " + e.getMessage());

} finally {

try {

if (reader != null) {

reader.close();

System.out.println("File closed successfully.");

}

} catch (IOException e) {

System.out.println("Error closing the file: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

}

}

In this example, we use the finally block to close FileReader after all file operations are complete. This occurs whether an exception was thrown or not. This approach to resource cleanup helps manage resources and makes our code more maintainable.

Throwing and Propagating Exceptions

Java includes the throw keyword which we can use to intentionally throw an exception. We can also use the throws keyword (note that this is different from throw) to propagate an exception to the calling method. This gives us great control and flexibility in creating our own exceptions or even rethrowing one that already exists.

Throwing Exceptions

Explicitly throwing an exception can be useful to enforce specific rules or generate custom error messages. Let us look at a simple example:

public class ExplicitThrowExample {

public static void main(String[] args) {

int age = 8;

if (age < 18) {

throw new IllegalArgumentException("You must be at least 18 to vote.");

}

}

}

In this example, we intentionally throw the IllegalArgumentException if the age is not at least 18. Here we can provide a contextual and meaningful error message to the user.

Propagating Exceptions

The concept of propagating exceptions, or exception propagation, is when we throw an exception to a higher-level method for handling. To better understand this, imagine a tiered help-desk support system:

  • Tier 1: This is the base support team. If they cannot solve the issue, they escalate it to Tier 2.
  • Tier 2: This team handles more complex problems. If the issue is still unresolved, it is escalated to Tier 3.
  • Tier 3: This is the highest level of support, with the most expertise.

In Java, we can propagate exceptions, just like support tickets can be escalated to the next tier. For Java, we escalate up the stack to a higher-level method. This is exception propagation.

Let’s look at how this is implemented in Java:

import java.io.*;

public class PropagationExample {

public static void main(String[] args) {

try {

readFile();

} catch (IOException e) {

System.out.println("The System caught an IOException: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

public static void readFile() throws IOException {

FileReader reader = new FileReader("ThisFileSimplyDoesNotExist.txt");

int character;

while ((character = reader.read()) != -1) {

System.out.print((char) character);

}

reader.close();

}

}

This example has the readFile method throw an IOException. In the case when the file is not found, the exception is propagated to the main() method, where the exception is caught and handled appropriately.

Rethrowing Exceptions

We can rethrow an exception by first catching it and then throwing it again to be handled by a higher-level method. Let us look at a rethrowing exception example:

import java.io.*;

public class RethrowExceptionExample {

public static void main(String[] args) {

try {

processFile();

} catch (IOException e) {

System.out.println("Exception handled here (in main()): " + e.getMessage());

}

}

public static void processFile() throws IOException {

try {

FileReader reader = new FileReader("NoFileToFind.txt");

reader.close();

} catch (IOException e) {

System.out.println("An error occurred: " + e.getMessage());

throw e; // Rethrow the exception to main()

}

}

}

This example code includes the processFile() method that catches an IOException. A simple output message is created and then it rethrows the exception to main(), which is one level up in the method hierarchy.

Creating Custom Exceptions

Just when you thought you knew everything about exceptions, Java gives us options. We can create custom exceptions by extending Java’s Exception class or its RuntimeException class. As you can learn in this section, custom exceptions can make our code more readable and empower our applications to handle specific error scenarios in a contextual manner.

The Importance of Creating Custom Exceptions

We can implement custom exceptions to represent application-specific errors; ones that Java does not already handle. When our exception names directly link to our error condition (for example, ZeroBalanceException), our application is said to be expressive. This makes our code easier to read and maintain. Furthermore, our error messages can be contextual, specific, and meaningful.

Defining Your Own Exception Classes

To create a custom exception, we need to either extend Java’s Exception class or its RuntimeException class. As you will remember from earlier in this chapter, the Exception class is for checked exceptions and the RuntimeException class is for unchecked exceptions. Let us look at an example:

public class ZeroBalanceException extends Exception {

public ZeroBalanceException(String message) {

super(message);

}

}

In the preceding example, we created the ZeroBalanceException class that extends Java’s Exception class. It contains a constructor and functionality for a custom error message. This gives us the ability to create a meaningful exception specifically for zero balance scenarios.

Throwing Custom Exceptions

Now that we have our custom exception, we can use the throw keyword to throw it in our code where appropriate. Here is how we might implement it:

public class UnitedElkBanking {

private double withdrawalAmount;

private double balance;

public UnitedElkBanking(double withdrawalAmount) {

this.withdrawalAmount = withdrawalAmount;

}

public void withdraw(double amount) throws ZeroBalanceException {

if (balance == 0) {

throw new ZeroBalanceException("Zero Balance. Unable to withdraw: " + withdrawalAmount);

}

}

}

In this example, the withdraw() method throws a ZeroBalanceException if the current balance equals zero.

Using Custom Exceptions for Specific Error Scenarios

In our loosely defined UnitedElkBanking example, we could write additional exceptions to include InsufficientFundsException and NegativeDepositException. Here are those classes:

public class NegativeDepositException extends Exception {

public NegativeDepositException(String message) {

super(message);

}

}

public class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception {

public InsufficientFundsException(String message) {

super(message);

}

}

Now, let us look at an example where all three custom exceptions are used in the sample application.

public class UnitedElkBanking2 {

private double balance;

public UnitedElkBanking2(double initialBalance) {

this.balance = initialBalance;

}

public void deposit(double amount) throws NegativeDepositException {

if (amount < 0) {

throw new NegativeDepositException("You cannot deposit a negative amount.");

}

balance += amount;

}

public void withdraw(double amount) throws InsufficientFundsException, ZeroBalanceException {

if (balance == 0) {

throw new ZeroBalanceException("Account balance is zero. Withdraw not permitted.");

}

if (amount > balance) {

throw new InsufficientFundsException("Insufficient funds. Available balance: " + balance);

}

balance -= amount;

}

public void checkBalance() {

System.out.println("Your current balance: $" + balance);

}

public static void main(String[] args) {

UnitedElkBanking2 account = new UnitedElkBanking2(100);

try {

// Attempt to deposit funds

account.deposit(50);

account.checkBalance();

// Attempt to withdraw more than the available balance to trigger an exception

account.withdraw(200);

} catch (NegativeDepositException e) {

System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());

} catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {

System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());

} catch (ZeroBalanceException e) {

System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());

}

// Attempt another withdrawal to check ZeroBalanceException handling

try {

account.withdraw(150);

account.checkBalance();

} catch (InsufficientFundsException e) {

System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());

} catch (ZeroBalanceException e) {

System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

}

Our UnitedElkBanking2 app, the second try block has catch clauses for InsufficientFundsException and ZeroBalanceException. These are the exceptions that the withdraw() method can throw. This program illustrates how we can easily create and implement custom exceptions to make our code expressive, readable, and maintainable.

Best Practices in Exception Handling

As you have had the opportunity to learn, exception handing is an important component of our applications. Handling exceptions certainly takes time, but it is not terribly difficult. The time spent on writing exception handling into our applications can save you time in the long run because your code will be more readable and maintainable.

In addition to handling errors being a best practice, many software development teams and organizations will require it of its developers. This is a habit you should work on. Let us look at several best practices based on industry norms:

  • Avoid Empty Blocks: Sometimes we work with templates or patterns such as try-catch blocks and, as we write our code, empty blocks might remain. This should be avoided – never catch an exception and fail to do anything with it.
  • Avoid Misuse: It can be tempting to use exception handling to control the flow of your program. That is not advisable. Use exception handing to maintain the normal application flow, not control it.
  • Avoid NullPointerException: The NullPointerException is not something you should try to catch. Instead, you use checks throughout your code, where appropriate, to ensure this exception is not thrown.
  • Be Contextual: When creating custom exceptions, make your user and log messages meaningful.
  • Be Efficiency-Minded: Exception handling is not free; it does have a performance overhead. Use tactics such as input and data validation before performing operations. Whenever possible avoid using exception handling in part of your code where high performance is critical.
  • Be Judicious: Use the throws clause to specify the exceptions that your methods can throw. This is okay but be careful of overusing it to declare every possible exception. This will make your code very difficult to read and maintain.
  • Cleanup Resources: Use the finally block to cleanup resources, as shown earlier in this chapter.
  • Customize: Wherever appropriate, use custom exceptions. This can give your application greater fidelity when handling exception scenarios not already handled by Java.
  • Log Exceptions: It is considered a best practice to log all exceptions. This is in addition to any on-screen or user-provided messaging.
  • Rethrow: When necessary, rethrow exceptions. For example, if you catch an exception that you cannot handle efficiently or effectively, you might consider rethrowing it to the calling method.
  • Use Specificity: Always catch the most specific exception possible instead of falling into the lazy trap of using the generic Exception class. We want to strive for precision in our error handling. Additionally, avoid catching overly broad exceptions such as Exception or Throwable. When we are more specific, we can better troubleshoot what caused the exception.

Following these best practices can help ensure your code is readable and maintainable, that your error messages are meaningful, and that your application flow will not be disrupted when an exception occurs.

Book Long Project

Armed with new knowledge of file and exception handling, you should be able to extend the SLAP LMS that you have worked on progressively in the previous chapters. It is time to add support for data persistence using file handling, allowing it to store and retrieve data between sessions. We will also implement exception handling to ensure file operation errors are gracefully managed.

This section details six tasks that you should complete to move your SLAP LMS project forward.

Implement Data Persistence for Courses and Students

Perform the following actions:

  1. Use the file handling techniques from this chapter to save and load key LMS data, such as course details and student enrollment. This will permit the LMS to retain information even after the application is closed.
  2. Create text files (courses.txt and students.txt) to store data in a simple, human-readable format.

Here is a sample code for saving data:

import java.io.BufferedWriter;

import java.io.FileWriter;

import java.io.IOException;

public class DataPersistenceWrite {

public static void saveCourseData(String courseName, int courseID) {

try (BufferedWriter writer = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("courses.txt", true))) {

writer.write(courseID + "," + courseName);

writer.newLine();

} catch (IOException e) {

System.err.println("Error saving course data: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

}

Loading Data from Files

Implement appropriate methods to load existing data into the LMS when the application starts. For example, have it read data from courses.txt to populate the course list. Do the same for students.txt.

Here is a sample code for loading data:

import java.io.BufferedReader;

import java.io.FileReader;

import java.io.IOException;

public class DataPersistenceLoad {

public static void loadCourseData() {

try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("courses.txt"))) {

String line;

while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {

String[] courseInfo = line.split(",");

System.out.println("Loaded course: ID " + courseInfo[0] + ", Name: " + courseInfo[1]);

}

} catch (IOException e) {

System.err.println("Error loading course data: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

}

Handling File-Related Exceptions

Add exception handling to manage potential file errors, such as missing files, access issues, and more. without causing the LMS to crash, use try-catch blocks to handle IOException and other specific exceptions related to file operations. For example, if courses.txt or students.txt is missing, prompt the user with an appropriate message.

Here is an example code to help you get started. Note, this is just a code snippet, not a completed class. It is simply a method that you will need to add to an appropriate class.

public static void loadStudentData() {

try {

BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("students.txt"));

// Reading logic here

} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {

System.out.println("Student file not found. A new file will be created upon saving.");

} catch (IOException e) {

System.err.println("Error reading student data: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

Serialization for Complex Data Storage

Implement serialization for storing objects. This will enable the SLAP LMS to handle complex data structures more efficiently. Specifically, use ObjectOuptutStream and ObjectInputStream to serialize and deserialize Course and Student objects. This functionality will be extremely important as the LMS evolves to a large-scale system.

Here is a sample code to help you get started:

import java.io.*;

public class Serialization {

public static void saveCourseObject(Course course) {

try (ObjectOutputStream oos = new ObjectOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("courses.ser"))) {

oos.writeObject(course);

} catch (IOException e) {

System.err.println("Error saving course object: " + e.getMessage());

}

}

public static Course loadCourseObject() {

try (ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream(new FileInputStream("courses.ser"))) {

return (Course) ois.readObject();

} catch (IOException | ClassNotFoundException e) {

System.err.println("Error loading course object: " + e.getMessage());

return null;

}

}

}

Custom Exceptions for LMS-Specific Errors

Create custom exceptions to handle LMS-specific issues to include CourseNotFoundException, StudentEnrollmentExceptiono, and others that you can think of. Implementing custom exceptions can make error handling more expressive and relevant to our LMS.

Here is a sample code to help you get started:

public class CourseNotFoundException extends Exception {

public CourseNotFoundException(String message) {

super(message);

}

}

Best Practices for Exception Management

Implement the following best practices:

  • Implement finally blocks or try-with-resources to ensure resources are closed properly. This should enhance resource management.
  • Log errors to a file for debugging and maintenance purposes. Make sure you append the log and not overwrite it.

Next Steps

In Chapter 6, Input/Output Streams, we will explore input/output streams in greater depth, enhancing data processing efficiency within the LMS. The goal will be to set up the LMS to handle larger data files and introduce more advanced data management techniques.

Conclusion

This chapter explored the essential aspects of file and exception handling in Java with a focus on how those elements contribute to building readable, maintainable, and efficient applications. Mastering file handling is a critical skill for all Java developers and is core to your application’s ability to read from and write to text and binary files, work with streams for improved performance, and efficiently store complex data using serialization and deserialization. Java’s exception handling ability empowers you to catch, manage, and respond to runtime errors, ensuring smooth application flow and enhancing the user experience.

File and exception handling are indispensable skills in real-world Java programming, where data persistence and error management are crucial. Adopting the best practices presented in this chapter can help make your applications more robust and also improve their maintainability.

In the next chapter, we will explore the concept of Input/Output (IO) streams in Java. These streams are essential for handling data input and output operations. You can learn about different types of streams, such as character streams and byte streams, and how to handle them to manage data flow in an application. The chapter also covers advanced I/O techniques to include buffered and data streams.

Points to Remember

  • A custom exception class can extend either Exception (for checked exceptions) or RuntimeException (for unchecked exceptions).
  • A file stream is a sequence of data from or to a file that supports input and output operations.
  • A finally block is always executed, regardless of whether an exception occurred, making it ideal for resource cleanup.
  • Avoid catching overly broad exceptions such as Exception or Throwable to enable more precise error handling.
  • Avoid using exception handling to control normal program flow; instead, use it for managing unexpected errors.
  • BufferedReader, when used with FileReader, enhances reading efficiency by buffering characters for larger files.
  • BufferedWriter is often used with FileWriter to increase the efficiency of writing large text files by buffering output.
  • Checked exceptions must be declared in a method’s throws clause or handled within a try-catch block.
  • Custom exceptions allow for more descriptive and specific error handling in applications.
  • DataInputStream and DataOutputStream enable reading and writing of primitive data types in binary format.
  • FileInputStream and FileOutputStream classes are used for reading from and writing to binary files.
  • FileNotFoundException and IOException are common checked exceptions that must be handled or declared in methods.
  • FileReader and FileWriter classes handle basic text file operations in Java, suitable for smaller text files.
  • IOException is a common superclass for exceptions that occur during I/O operations.
  • InputStream and OutputStream are the base classes in Java for handling input and output streams.
  • NullPointerException should be avoided by implementing appropriate checks rather than catching it as an exception.
  • ObjectInputStream and ObjectOutputStream classes are used for deserialization and serialization, respectively, enabling object data storage and retrieval.
  • Propagating exceptions allows a method to throw an exception to be handled by a higher-level method in the call stack.
  • Rethrowing an exception can be useful when a lower-level method cannot handle an error effectively and needs to pass it up the call stack.
  • Serialization converts a Java object into a byte stream for storage or transmission, while deserialization restores it to its original state.
  • Specific feedback and contextual error messages help improve the user experience when handling exceptions.
  • The BufferedReader class reads input efficiently by buffering characters, improving performance for large files.
  • The finally block is commonly used for resource cleanup, such as closing files or network and database connections.
  • The try-catch block in Java allows for detecting, capturing, and handling exceptions, preventing program crashes.
  • The throws keyword in method signatures specifies exceptions that a method might throw, which can be handled by the calling method.
  • Throwing exceptions explicitly with the throw keyword enables us to enforce specific application rules, such as age restrictions and balance constraints.
  • To prevent performance impacts, avoid using exceptions in high-frequency code paths or in performance-critical sections.
  • Use custom exceptions for more meaningful, context-specific error messages that can aid in debugging and user support.
  • Use multiple catch blocks to handle different exception types distinctly, providing tailored responses for each error type.
  • Using try-with-resources is recommended for managing resources, as it automatically closes resources when the block completes.

Multiple-Choice Questions

  1. Which class is typically used to read from a text file in Java?
    1. FileWriter
    2. FileReader
    3. BufferedWriter
    4. BufferedReader
  2. What is the purpose of the finally block in exception handling?
    1. To catch specific exceptions
    2. To execute code only if an exception occurs
    3. To ensure code is executed regardless of exceptions
    4. To rethrow exceptions to higher-level methods
  3. Which of the following is true about custom exceptions in Java?
    1. They cannot extend RuntimeException
    2. They are only used for checked exceptions
    3. They are created by extending Exception or RuntimeException
    4. All of the above
  4. Which method is used in BufferedWriter to create a new line in the output file?
    1. writeLine()
    2. addNewLine()
    3. nextLine()
    4. newLine()
  5. What is exception propagation in Java?
    1. Passing an exception to a higher-level method for handling
    2. Passing an exception to a lower-level method for handling
    3. Automatically resolving exceptions during runtime
    4. Using catch blocks to handle multiple exceptions

Answers

  1. b
  2. c
  3. c
  4. d
  5. a

Questions

  3. How does serialization contribute to data storage and retrieval in Java?

  9. Discuss the importance of the finally block in resource management. Share a scenario where failing to release resources properly could lead to serious issues in an application.

Key Terms

  • ArithmeticException: An unchecked exception thrown when an invalid arithmetic operation, such as division by zero, is attempted.
  • BufferedReader: A class used to read text from an input stream, buffering characters for efficient reading, especially with large files.
  • BufferedWriter: A class used to write text to an output stream, buffering characters to improve write performance.
  • Checked Exception: An exception that must be either caught in a try-catch block or declared in the method’s throws clause.
  • Custom Exception: A user-defined exception that extends Java’s Exception or RuntimeException classes to provide specific error handling.
  • DataInputStream: A class that allows reading primitive data types in binary format, commonly used with binary files.
  • DataOutputStream: A class that enables writing primitive data types in binary format, used to save data in binary files.
  • Deserialization: The process of converting a byte stream back into an object, often used to retrieve data stored in serialized form.
  • Exception Propagation: The mechanism by which an exception is passed up the method call stack to a higher-level method that can handle it.
  • FileInputStream: A class used for reading data from binary files.
  • FileNotFoundException: A checked exception thrown when an attempt is made to open a file that does not exist.
  • FileOutputStream: A class used for writing bytes to binary files.
  • FileReader: A class that reads character-based data from a file, often used for reading text files.
  • FileWriter: A class that writes character-based data to a file, commonly used for writing text files.
  • Finally Block: A block in a try-catch-finally structure that executes regardless of whether an exception occurs, often used for resource cleanup.
  • IllegalArgumentException: An unchecked exception thrown when a method receives an argument that is inappropriate or invalid.
  • IOException: A superclass for exceptions that occur during input/output operations, such as file handling errors.
  • NullPointerException: An unchecked exception thrown when an application attempts to use an object reference that has not been initialized.
  • ObjectInputStream: A class used for deserialization, converting a byte stream back into an object.
  • ObjectOutputStream: A class used for serialization, converting an object into a byte stream for storage or transmission.
  • Propagation: The process of passing an exception up the call stack to be handled by a higher-level method.
  • Resource Cleanup. The practice of releasing resources, such as closing files or connections, to prevent resource leaks.
  • Serialization. The process of converting an object into a byte stream, allowing it to be saved to a file or transmitted.
  • Throwing Exceptions: Using the throw keyword to explicitly signal an exception, often to enforce a rule or condition.
  • Try-With-Resources: A statement that automatically closes resources when the try block completes, contributing to efficient resource management.
  • Unchecked Exception: An exception that occurs at runtime and does not need to be declared or caught, often due to programming errors.

Exercises

Exercise 1: Reading from a Text File

Use both FileReader and BufferedReader to read and display the content. Test your program by adding additional lines to the text file.

Exercise 2: Writing to a Text File
